Notably, a 2020 paper demonstrated that a frozen backbone with 1000 Neurons was capable of performing well across tasks in the Split-Wild scenario for the 80-20 task split on the CIFAR-100 dataset. However, this outstanding performance seemed implausibly good and warranted further investigation. We attempted to replicate this outcome but discovered that the same method yielded significantly inferior results. In order to explain these differing outcomes, we analyzed multiple factors including dataset preprocessing, label quality, and evaluation methodology. Ultimately, we found no clear explanation for the initial encouraging findings. Consequently, we believe it is unwise to rely on methods that, like this one, challenge the necessity of post-pretraining training for continual learning without a more thorough understanding of why they work in certain instances. We hope that our research will guide others in pursuing a more comprehensive exploration of these complex issues. Approximately nine years ago, Igamberdiev and Jia introduced the concept of Lipschitz games, a broad category of games that includes as subcategories partial equilibrium, partial competition, and general equilibrium games under specific inter-agent connectivity requirements. Their work established a significant connection between the property of unique equilibria and the structure of the game's payoff functions in particular contexts. In the present work, we address the open question they posed and identify lower complexity bounds for the family of Lipschitz games, demonstrating that both the number of questions needed to determine whether a strategy profile constitutes an equilibrium and the number needed to determine whether a strategy profile is the unique equilibrium all increase in proportion to n log n in the general case of n-player games. Furthermore, we observe that this improvement is specifically tailored to accommodate the substantial impact of external information availability on decision-making in the context of Lipschitz games. By contrast, we note that in the scenario where players have perfect information about the game's structure, the complexity of finding equilibria can be determined with a fixed number of queries. Additionally, we provide a corresponding lower bound for the complexity of finding the maximum equilibrium payoff, and we show that this result holds for both the Kuhn-Tucker and Koller-Shmueli learning models. Finally, we explore the applicability of these results to other types of games. In the case of games where the same set of agents compete in multiple stages, we establish a lower complexity bound under the Kuhn-Tucker model. On the other hand, we present an algorithm that finds a Nash equilibrium efficiently in games with external information under the Koller-Shmueli model. However, we note that this result may be contingent on additional assumptions about the game's structure. Lastly, we provide a generalization of our main complexity lower bound to a broader class of games and establish a new lower complexity bound for finding a co-Nash equilibrium in games with external information. This work is a full extension of our previous research on this topic and builds upon our initial findings. All the results presented here have been formally verified through proper proofs. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil phenomena, providing insights that could be useful for developing new methods of controlling ultracold atomic processes with light. Furthermore, this system can serve as a simple model for investigating photon recoil effects in broader contexts. 
We have also extended the scope of our research to include multiple light field components, as demonstrated in our second paper in this series. 
In our experiment, the frequency shift induced by the interaction proved difficult to measure precisely due to a phenomenon related to photon recoil, which resulted in a spreading out of the absorption pattern beyond our expected resolution. This limitation led us to refine our experimental technique by increasing the thickness of our atomic sample, enabling us to precisely measure the frequency shift for the first time. This achievement allowed us to confirm our theoretical model and make an accurate measurement of the relevant decay constant, although it fell short of our resolution by about an order of magnitude. 
As a side benefit, our research produced a high-precision measurement of the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. 
Our findings have implications for any experiment that measures the transmission of a light beam as it passes through a cloud of ultracold atoms, particularly when using a single light beam and monitoring the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam. 
In our case, the difficulty we encountered led us to modify our experimental approach by changing the intensity of our light source, as well as the thickness and temperature of our atomic sample.

When subjected to high forces, the majority of dense mixtures thicken exponentially, exhibiting a sudden and drastic response. This phenomenon of shear thickening poses a problem for robots and machines interacting with these materials, as even minor shocks can cause the materials to stiffen excessively. Despite its widespread occurrence, the physics driving shear thickening remains not fully understood, as it cannot be predicted by existing theories. Researchers have proposed competing mechanisms to explain this phenomenon, but they often require artificial adjustments and do not account for the universal pattern that has gone unnoticed until now. In a breakthrough discovery, scientists found that regardless of the specific materials used, the degree of thickening is always proportional to the distance from the critical shock required to initiate the transition. This breakthrough finding provides a crucial basis for developing a new theory that could potentially explain the underlying physics of shear thickening. By modeling their data, researchers were able to use this proportionality to create a map that predicts the point at which the material will suddenly thicken when subjected to different shock conditions. This groundbreaking study, which provides the first detailed look at the physics of shear thickening, could have a significant impact on the design of machines that interact with dense materials. Furthermore, this breakthrough may also be applicable to other complex transitions that have gone unstudied with modern instruments.

This gap exists across multiple NLP domains, including but not limited to, sentence representation evaluation, machine translation assessment, and semantic classification reviews. The existing approach uses a basic test statistic to compare system performance, but this method falls short because it doesn't account for the inherent structure within data sets. To address these limitations, we propose an advanced paired-permutation test methodology that takes into consideration the organizational structure of datasets. This proposed method is applicable to a broad range of statistical tests and can be executed with optimal precision at a fixed cost of serial testing on a single dataset. GNNs utilize node features and graph structure to classify nodes based on their properties and relationships, but complex models can be computationally expensive and difficult to understand. We introduced the concept of learning sparsification for GNNs, reducing model complexity and improving performance by selectively retaining critical edge connections and node features. A novel framework was developed to achieve this by optimizing a sparsification loss function that refines models on a subset of data with reduced computational costs. Notably, this framework facilitates model interpretability by identifying important edge connections and node features that contribute to predictions. Experimental results on diverse datasets demonstrate improved computational efficiency, enhanced performance, and increased interpretability of GNNs. Interestingly, our approach was also found to be a effective method for removing noisy edge connections and node features. Building on previous findings, we observed in Part I that compact, singular areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature can be conformally deformed to reveal related minimal geometries sharing key characteristics. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets affecting these geometries. This achievement enables us to establish that the removed sets, once normalized, also possess minimal volume 1 feature and Poincare inequality validity, ultimately enabling the extension of the conformal deformation to the non-singular areas within the original manifold. This advancement has significant implications for the application of the Almgren-Shanmugam compactness theorem. In particular, this allows us to prove that compact areas within a manifold of positive scalar curvature cannot have a minimal volume 1 feature and cannot validate Poincare inequalities on an set with a positive measure. This result has far-reaching consequences and can be used to prove Nirenberg's conjecture concerning the rigidity of areas with positive scalar curvature. This approach to proving conjectures concerning the rigidity of areas with positive scalar curvature also raises the question of whether such results can be achieved under the weaker assumption that minimal volumes are bounded. This question has implications for the broader theory of geometric variational problems. This note provides a detailed overview of the strategy employed to solve problems related to the rigidity of areas with positive scalar curvature. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. In addition, a decentralized version of MEF is introduced, enabling broader applicability across various scheduling scenarios. Experimental results, comprising power management in adaptive electric vehicles, showcase the capabilities of this approach in real-world settings. Furthermore, theoretical bounds on the MEF distribution are provided, along with an exploration of different reinforcement learning hyperparameters and their impacts on PPC performance. These findings contribute valuable insights to the design of learning-driven control systems. Overall, this paper presents an innovative solution for the efficient real-time management of controllable loads through learning-driven PPC, enabling a more adaptable and responsive interaction with complex energy systems. This work also establishes a foundation for further exploration into the interplay between exploration and exploitation in the context of MEF. As a complementary component, we have made our implementation publicly available for dissemination and utilization by other researchers. This code is openly accessible via an associated GitHub link. Initially, we consider the most relevant effective operators affecting the Higgs sector and investigate their impact on double Higgs production. Edge computing and machine learning are experiencing rapid growth and their integration is gaining momentum.  Despite this trend, a persistent challenge hindering wider adoption revolves around reducing data transmission between the edge and the cloud.  To tackle this issue, techniques such as edge processing, data compression, and encryption are being explored.  Another potential strategy involves modifying applications and systems to respond to events rather than process continuous data streams.  This paper introduces the concept of an application data flow graph, a tool that helps identify opportunities for improving applications by shifting the focus from processing streams to processing events.  To utilize this approach, developers need three key pieces of information: 1) an understanding of how to define an application data flow graph, 2) methods for evaluating the effectiveness of edge processing, and 3) techniques for optimizing application data flow graphs.  This paper provides examples of edge applications, shows how an application data flow graph can be constructed, presents a proposed evaluation framework, and discusses future directions for research in this area.  We anticipate this work will spark interesting discussions about the future of edge applications, and we hope to encourage others to explore ways to improve the efficiency of these systems.  We have made our work openly available on GitHub under an permissive license, and we have also created a demonstration available online.  On this note, we would like to invite others to collaborate with us and help us move this research forward. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely CP violation and rare decays, within charm and beauty meson systems. This study reports the findings of distinct searches carried out by ATLAS. For example, D^0-D^0 mixing and CP violation in D^0 decays were investigated. Additionally, direct and indirect CP violation in D^0 decays to final states involving kaons and pions were examined. Furthermore, rare decays of D^0 and B^0_s mesons to muons and electrons were probed for signs of supersymmetric or multi-lepton New Physics contributions. A comprehensive summary of all results is provided in this report. Moreover, a discussion on the further statistical combination of several results as well as impending sensitivity in these searches at the ATLAS experiment in future LHC runs is included. As of now, no indication of New Physics has been discovered; hence, strict limits on New Physics coefficients can be deduced from these searches. In particular, in D^0 decays to final states involving kaons and pions, the measured value of the direct CP violation coefficient differs from the known value of 0.025 ± 0.001 by a margin of 1.7 standard deviations. For D^0 decays to final states involving pions, the measured value of the mixing coefficient differs from the known value of 0.467 ± 0.013 by a margin of 2.8 standard deviations. In D^0 decays to final states involving kaons, the measured value of the CP violation coefficient differs from the known value of -0.015 ± 0.003 by a margin of 1.9 standard deviations. In B^0_s decays to final states involving muons, the measured value of the branching fraction coefficient is 3.35 ± 0.20, which exceeds the standard model prediction by a margin of 1.3 standard deviations. In B^0_s decays to final states involving electrons, the measured value of the direct CP violation coefficient is -0.59 ± 0.25, which does not diverge from 0 by a significant margin. The development of highly advanced driving systems relies heavily on the creation of realistic traffic scenarios to test their capabilities. Current approaches often limit the process to configuring existing dataset attributes or manually inputting road characteristics and vehicle positions, which is not only time-consuming but also fails to account for the dynamic changes these scenes inevitably undergo during simulated extended periods of time. In response, we've designed SceneGen, an end-to-end traffic scenario model that produces fresh data with each run. By utilizing latent vector representations of driving principles and incorporating spatial awareness through multiple layer grid filters, SceneGen efficiently generates detailed scenes complete with participating vehicles, their corresponding attributes, and accurately calculated positions. By leveraging both scene-behavior preservation, layer filters, and spatial rejection sampling techniques, SceneGen is capable of producing highly realistic traffic scenarios that mimic actual dataset distributions. With only a small additional training requirement, SceneGen outperforms baseline methods in evaluation metrics such as ADE, FD, and R-50 on the Argoverse benchmark dataset. Furthermore, SceneGen demonstrates superior performance in multi-stage evaluation scenarios. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, the article provides a framework for developing flexible Krylov methods that preserve specific properties of the underlying PDE solution. Several examples, including the conservative system, Friedrichs' model, Navier-Stokes equations, and nonlinear heat equation, are used to illustrate the method's effectiveness, showing that it can provide a viable alternative to explicit time-stepping methods for preserving certain properties. The article also explores the impact of different preconditioners on the method's convergence, highlighting the importance of choice of preconditioner in determining whether or not the property-preserving property is maintained. For autonomous navigation, accurate scene flow estimation is crucial. We discover that pre-trained metric learning models, widely used in this task, are prone to bias because they're often trained on datasets that include misleading annotations from untrusted sources. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel self-supervised adversarial metric learning framework to refine the models' performance. This framework enables the model to learn from unseen categories in real-world scenarios through a two-stage process. Initially, we develop a feature extraction model that utilizes pure metric learning to recognize categories from which high-quality annotations are obtained. Subsequently, we integrate an unsupervised contrastive learning component that encourages the model to learn distinctive scene features to accurately predict scene flow without relying on category labels. This results in a robust model that performs exceptionally well in self-supervised scene flow estimation tasks, outperforming baseline models and surpassing the benchmark on the KITTI dataset. This paper introduces a new method for automating system call filtering in Linux, specifically tailored for Linux Virtual Machines. This approach is designed to detect potential security threats and prevent malicious activities from specific system calls. We have developed Timeloops, an automated system call learning tool based on this method, using a combination of static analysis and runtime data. This study adapts the partial batch maximum likelihood (PMBM) filter to estimate the number of active sources and their locations using a grid-based model for unobserved time intervals. Initially, the observed regions are divided into a grid for all time steps up to T, with further refinement possible for time steps beyond T. At each step, only the grid cells containing observed regions contribute to the maximum likelihood function, with an emphasis on estimating the number of active sources and their locations within those cells. Unlike the standard batch maximum likelihood (BMM) filter, this approach doesn't require all time steps to have equally fine-grained grids; instead, refinements can be made dynamically based on incoming sensor data. This method is tested on a sensor management scenario with limited and interfering sensors, with the goal of optimizing the number of active sources and their locations within a bounded area. Results show that this algorithm effectively estimates the number of active sources and their locations, leading to optimal results in a subsequent competitive subspace classification (CSC) filter trial. Furthermore, this algorithm leads to more sensors being turned off in the CSC trial compared to a simpler method. This algorithm can also handle a larger number of time steps with reduced complexity compared to the standard BMM filter. Additionally, it was found that using a finer grid at step T provides the best results in terms of accuracy. This method assumes that the motion model for the sources can be represented by switching between distinct velocities, with no limit on the number of possible velocities. This study provides a framework for applying this algorithm in a CSC filter setup, but does not include results from the CSC filter itself. This is due to an issue with the implementation of the CSC filter's decision logic, specifically with regards to handling the complexities of partial batch sizing. This complexity arises from the delay in origin modeling, which makes some sources considered active by the CSC filter actually inactive, and vice versa. This discrepancy needs to be addressed in future research. This study also explores different ways to handle the delay in origin modeling, with an attempt to delay the refinement of the grid model until more sensor measurements become available. This strategy, however, led to inaccurate estimates of the number of active sources and their locations. Another approach tried setting the refined grid model's start time to the point at which the delay became known, but this resulted in the failure to detect some sources. This study concludes by outlining several potential future research directions. It suggests testing this algorithm in scenarios with varying time steps, as well as integrating it with more complex motion models.

Despite advancements in physics-based migration techniques such as reverse time migration (RTM), its computational expense and requirement for accurate source information limits its broad adoption.  Key factors affecting RTM efficiency include the need for multiple RTMs to account for unknown source functions and limited accuracy due to approximate extended source effects during data acquisition.  We investigate an alternative approach by directly solving the inverse problem using the wave equation with assumed receiver functions and a mathematical formulation that incorporates the data and wave equation equation constraints through Lagrange multipliers.  Formulating the inverse problem in this way yields an iterative process that involves solving a well-posed wave equation optimization problem at each step, for which stable and high-resolution solutions exist.  We propose using a gradient-based algorithm with an implicit operator formulation that can be efficiently computed using a limited number of forward and adjoint time-domain wave equation simulations.  We also describe a computational framework that can be scaled up using a distributed memory approach, based on solving small-scale, high-resolution adjoint and forward problems in parallel.  Our results show that this approach results in highly resolved and accurate estimates of complex source wavelet and subsurface reflectivity at once, for an idealized seismic acquisition setting but with real data examples in development.  We plan to explore future extensions of this method with other optimization algorithms and with more realistic data models that account for extended sources, rough sea surface, and marine seismic data acquisition.  We anticipate that this technique will be important for enhancing low-quality data, improving resolution in complex media, and increasing the resolution of seismic surveys with sparse and irregular source and receiver configurations. Current approaches have used maximum likelihood estimation and negative log likelihood to build the model, but this does not guarantee the best performance. This paper introduces a new Place Recognizer model based on classification principles, known as the AttDLNet, which uses an attention-based deep learning network to identify a destination point's three-dimensional coordinates. The attention-based approach allows the network to focus on specific local LiDAR information when recognizing places, and this leads to better performance than traditional methods. The results show that this novel approach outperforms existing methods using a comprehensive evaluation protocol. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Conversely, the compressibility is proportional to the density of states at the Fermi level and increases in direct proportion to the temperature. A critical temperature-related phenomenon observed in our model is the sharp decrease in screening length with rising temperature, eventually reaching a point where the thermal capacity over estimates the compressibility by a factor of 2 pi. This theoretical framework can be adapted to other two-dimensional materials possessing close-to-perfect Dirac band structures. Due to their accessibility without the need to establish new connections, post offices, and the ease with which messages can be sent, they have become an appealing target for cyber attackers. Institutional email networks hold significant value in representing academic collaboration networks and national innovation capacities. In the case of R&D collaborations, the visibility they provide, combined with the centrality of key nodes, can offer valuable insights to potential threats and promote the overall security of the network. In the present study, a Markov Chain-based approach is introduced to examine the structural changes within a research collaboration network and the spread of malicious information. In addition, a Vulnerability Analysis module is developed to evaluate the impact of these changes and the reach of the cyber attack on the network. Through its implementation at Tsinghua University using email data from 2003 to 2012, the proposed method demonstrates its capability to identify critical components of a network, such as central nodes and weak links, as well as their effectiveness in network defense strategies. In the case of Tsinghua University, the results indicate that the network exhibits resistance to the spread of malicious information and the influence of key nodes has a lasting impact. Furthermore, a comparison with historical data reveals that the network's defense against cyber threats has evolved over time, with a marked decrease in its vulnerability occurring in 2006. In the later stages, the network's central nodes become less resistant to the spread of malicious information. In the conclusion, the approach presented in this study can be applied to other collaboration networks and email networks within institutions, and its simplicity allows it to be adaptable to networks with changing dynamics. In the context of Tsinghua University's email data, this study provides valuable insights that can be leveraged to inform the development of more effective network defense strategies. In the process, a Tsinghua University dataset with distinct characteristics is created, and the results obtained from this study can be utilized to formulate policy recommendations aimed at promoting a positive work environment and preventing the overloading of central nodes with non-essential information. In the long-term, this dataset can be employed to monitor the evolution of collaboration networks and the impact of network defense strategies on the prevention of malicious information spread. In the later stages of this research, the focus will shift towards analyzing the relationship between the structural changes within collaboration networks, the information spread, and the impact of network dynamics on the performance of key nodes. Building spallation neutron sources like the Aberdeen Tunnel laboratory requires precise understanding of neutron interaction with concrete, especially for moderator materials like polystyrene. However, there's a lack of suitable detectors for accurately measuring the characteristics of spallation neutrons. To bridge this gap, we propose developing a specialized detector system utilizing plastic scintillators and a novel approach to neutron reconstruction. Utilizing a large-area plastic scintillator and a central hydrogen-filled crystal, we aim to track slow neutrons and accurately calculate their energy based on scintillation light characteristics. A mathematical model predicting energy output based on neutron velocity will facilitate broad energy spectrum measurement. Furthermore, we plan to combine these detectors with previously developed hydrogen-filled stop detectors to enhance tracking capabilities and reconstruct the trajectory of incoming protons, thereby inferring the origin and characteristics of produced neutrons. This device will significantly contribute to gathering crucial data essential for optimizing the performance of future spallation neutron sources. Additionally, it will have the ability to monitor neutron flux and energy output, in addition to providing insights into proton stopping depth and the scattering cross-section of protons, which can be applied to various applications beyond neutron production, such as radiotherapy treatment. We're in the process of building a working prototype of this device and anticipate it will be operational by the end of this year. Initial test results with slow neutrons are also presented in this report. Overall, this novel detector design will serve as a model for creating suitable devices for measuring the characteristics of spallation neutrons in other facilities. Thousands of exoplanets have been discovered using this approach. However, there are still many unanswered questions regarding the properties of exoplanets, particularly their compositions and atmospheres. The Kepler space telescope's ability to collect transit data was a major breakthrough, enabling the analysis of planetary systems similar to our own. Its success has paved the way for the next-generation TESS telescope, which will allow for a more in-depth study of planetary systems similar to our own. The TESS-Keck Survey has been designed to complement the TESS telescope by using radial velocity measurements from ground-based telescopes to analyze the composition and atmosphere of transiting planets. The TESS-Keck Survey consists of three main areas of study: analyzing the composition and atmosphere of small planets; identifying features in the composition and atmosphere of larger planets; and determining the orbital alignment of planets. Determining the physical characteristics of M-dwarfs is crucial for studying these popular low-mass stars. Although M-dwarfs make up three-fourths of the galaxies nearest to our own, the most precise method of analyzing their properties, spectroscopic star-to-star comparison, is limited in effectiveness due to the cool, faint nature of these stars when viewed from Earth. As a result, researchers typically rely on photometric methods or genealogical information to estimate their stellar parameters, which are often inaccurate when applied generally. In an effort to break down these limitations, we present a new sample of 289 M-dwarfs that have been observed in the ultraviolet spectrum. Using the most detailed analysis ever of these stars, we executed a comprehensive assessment of their atmospheric parameters, including temperature, surface gravity, and metal content. This process involved a feed-forward neural network that was trained on a subset of the data and validated on the remainder. The resulting parameters were compared to those calculated through other methods such as the stellar atmospheric model, and we discovered notable discrepancies in the estimates. For instance, the average temperature of the M-dwarfs in our sample was found to be 3793 K, which is significantly lower than the generally accepted value of 3750 K. We also discovered a notable relationship between the estimated and actual atmospheric parameters of these stars. As we continue to gather more UV data on these stars, this relationship will be useful in recovering the actual properties of the stars, even if the analysis is based on less precise methods. Additionally, our selection of field M-dwarfs in our sample allows us to remove any biases that can affect property measurements, making them applicable across the broader field M-dwarf population. As we move forward in this study series, we will utilize these accurately determined stellar parameters to analyze the diverse range of exoplanets that orbit these low-mass stars. This includes both small, terrestrial planets as well as large gas giants, and will provide a uniform analysis of all the planets within a given system. This integrated approach will enable us to compare the diverse planetary populations that exist across the broader universe. This will be especially useful in searching for any life that may exist elsewhere in the vast universe. This study is an important step in launching a comprehensive study of low-mass stars and their planetary systems. The study of computable infinite words through formal language recognition has been extensively explored. However, the field lacks a comprehensive framework for synthesizing computable methods from specifications written in context-free grammars. To address this gap, we introduce a novel approach where we develop context-free grammars that generate computable infinite words according to a specific computable function. Building on this foundation, we further explore the generation of computable infinite words from non-deterministic context-free grammars and even from context-free grammars with counter capabilities. Notably, our methods are underpinned by a novel technique for translating two-dimensional context-free grammars into equivalent one-dimensional pushdown automata with counter capabilities. This research framework opens up new directions for the analysis of computable infinite words generated by computable methods from specifications expressed as context-free grammars. Specifically, we investigate decision-making problems related to whether a given computable method is deterministic, and whether two computable methods are equivalent. These results demonstrate the practical utility of our synthesis methods and showcase the computational complexity of the issues they raise. Finally, one of our open questions touches on the relationship between our approach and the broader field of computable logic in the finite case. On the other hand, our approach raises intricate questions related to the translation of specific context-free grammars and whether certain computable methods can be achieved. Additionally, our research introduces the concept of synthesizing computable methods with respect to a specific computable function, leading to several new direction for exploration. Furthermore, we explore how our methods handle the case of computable methods with a memory, specifically pushdown storage, and even counter capabilities. On top of that, our research also raises complex issues regarding whether a given computable method is deterministic or not, and whether two given computable methods are equivalent. To analyze the impact of spin-orbit coupling on superconducting electrons, we developed a BCS-Bogoliubov approach for a general nematic superconducting state. By investigating the interaction of an external magnetic field with the superconducting state, we discovered its influence on the quasiparticle energy and the superconducting order parameter. A notable result emerges when the magnetic field aligns with the long axis of the superconducting state, where it causes the superconducting state to transition from a chiral nematic phase to an orthorhombic phase characterized by zero Berry phase. A contrasting response occurs when the magnetic field is perpendicular to the long axis, resulting in a chiral orthorhombic phase transforming into a higher-energy state and giving rise to a Berry phase-driven paramagnetic response. This effect could be experimentally measured through magnetic susceptibility in metals possessing significant spin-orbit coupling, such as certain heavy transition metals or actinides. A numerical simulation is provided for the Pauli paramagnetic energy correction within the orthorhombic phase state in a representative heavy fermion metal, UTe$_2$. We believe that our approach has the potential to significantly expand the range of corrective feedback that can be effectively used to robot learning. Further research by the same team was published in 2000, along with C. S. Cockell, who utilized the data in his 2003 book "The Rockwalker." A critical aspect from these studies involves regions on the Moon with varying cross-sectional areas, which were determined by analyzing the lunar regolith's impact on the NEAR spacecraft's trajectory as it descended. The discovery of the T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with up-to-date data has been lacking. Employing the APOLLO code, a cutting-edge spectral retrieval method developed for wide-area surveys, we investigated the atmospheric properties of GJ 229B. By analyzing near-infrared spectra from 1.0 to 2.5 um, the code identified 14 key molecular features, allowing for a comprehensive analysis of H2O, CH4, CO, CO2, H- (protons), and temperature trends across the atmosphere. Our results indicate that water covers the planet's surface and fills its atmosphere, with little to no evidence of other molecules; however, more sensitive data might reveal additional information. Furthermore, our data suggest a temperature gradient, potentially indicating atmospheric circulation. Nonetheless, more precise observations are necessary to confirm these findings and gain a deeper understanding of this mysterious world. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained imitation learning tasks that only require matching demonstrated trajectories, learning from demonstrated trajectories with complex constraints poses significant challenges. In particular, demonstrating how to navigate through narrow passages requires careful planning to avoid collision with obstacles, making this task nonlinear non-Euclidean. To tackle such complexities, we propose a novel imitation learning framework called EKMP that generalizes beyond simple boundary constraint tasks. It accounts for linear and nonlinear constraints, as well as obstacles, to efficiently learn from demonstrated trajectories with complex constraints. Our results show that our framework outperforms a stateless model-based method and a neural network-based method that can learn from multiple demonstrations. Additionally, EKMP exhibits superior performance when compared to a state-based method that can learn from a single demonstration with no obstacles. Correspondingly, robust zero-energy Majorana fermion modes appear at the ends of a 1D Rashba Hubbard chain connected to a normal Rashba chain, serving as a hallmark for the STSFS phase. Calculations of the Rashba Hubbard model using the exact diagonalization method for a normal 1D chain and a 2D Rashba Hubbard tunnel coupled to normal Rashba leads also confirm the existence of the STSFS phase. Moreover, analysis of the Rashba Hubbard model's phase diagram reveals that the STSFS phase is separated from a Rashba Hubbard chain's $4\kappa$-fold degenerate superflow phase by a domain wall, both sharing a common boundary at a cusp point. Critically, the Mermin-Wang string order parameter serves as a distinguished probe for the STSFS and $4\kappa$-fold degenerate superflow phases. High-speed rotation in the Rashba Hubbard model leads to the onset of the STSFS phase at a small rotation speed compared to its classical-damped counterpart. High temperature doping in the Rashba Hubbard model results in the onset of the STSFS phase at a high doping concentration compared to its charge-density-wave counterpart. Lastly, the topological nature of the STSFS phase in the Rashba Hubbard model makes it susceptible to non-Abelian operations. Collective dipole approximation leads to an exact Rashba Hubbard Hamiltonian and the onset of the STSFS phase in the Rashba Hubbard model, a phenomenon also observed in its equivalent form, the one-dimensional Rashba Huberd model. Consequently, this provides a novel means to achieve the STSFS phase in atomic gases using optical lattices. Ultimately, this exact correspondence between the Rashba Hubbard Hamiltonian and its dipole approximation provides a means to achieve the exact STSFS phase in atomic gases using optical lattices. We designed a distinct binary star pattern, which we call "Binary Asters", consisting of a central pair of stars surrounded by symmetric reflex circles. This configuration produces notable effects on the brightness variations of the binary asterism, specifically generating irregular light curve shapes that could help identify them. Employing mathematical modeling and light curve simulations, we established the theoretical light curve characteristics of Binary Asters in different orientations. By comparing these predictions with actual data from the Pan-STARRS1 survey, we developed a method for detecting these rare phenomena based on their irregular light curve patterns. This approach allowed us to find several potential Binary Aster candidates across various orientations. Additionally, our research provided statistical evidence that Binary Asters exhibit a preference for specific mass ratios and small orbital periods. Furthermore, our findings indicated that Binary Asters exhibit distinct brightness variation amplitudes, likely influenced by their orientation and alignment with the observer's view. By defining Binary Asters as a separate category of binary stars, our discovery sheds new light on the diversity of these celestial bodies and the need for a more flexible classification system. The Southern Atlantic rift system, extending from 3°N to 50°S latitude, developed as a divergent plate boundary where Africa and America separated into two distinct continental plates. Studies using magnetic anomalies have outlined the rift's kinematic history, mapping ancient spreading centers and determining past sea-floor spreading rates. Initially, the rift system expanded at a rate of approximately 1-2 cm/yr between Africa and America, with some areas showing varying rates. Near 10 million years ago, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge shifted towards the African continent as the rift system expanded asymetrically, resulting in increased sea-floor spreading rates in the southern section, reaching as high as 3 cm/yr between 10°S and 30°S. This shift had a significant impact on global climate patterns and ocean circulation systems. Today, the Southern Atlantic rift system exhibits a central axis with a wide continental margin, with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge narrowing to 100 km in width between 10°S and 30°S. We propose the use of $k_\perp$-dependent coherent and coherent-plus-incoherent particle distribution functions, leading to improved explanations of observations made with RHIC and the LHC. These functions accurately account for collective effects at mid and large angles, and are derived from first principles using an interacting quasiparticle model that incorporates collective interactions. By applying these functions in a collective model, we achieve a good fit to data from 200 GeV and 5.02 TeV $p+p$ and $p+Au$ collisions, including measurements of elliptic flow coefficients $v_2\{2C\}$, $v_2\{4C\}$, and $v_2\{EP\}$. Notably, our approach provides a clear distinction between in-medium scattering rates and collective flow components. We demonstrate that the proposed $k_\perp$-dependent distribution functions are relevant at both RHIC and LHC energies for $p+p$ and $p+A$ collisions. We also establish a useful relationship between these functions and elliptic flow coefficients $v_2\{2C\}$ and $v_2\{4C\}$. Furthermore, we find that the proposed incoherent parton scattering rate is insufficient to explain data from 200 GeV $p+Au$ collisions, indicating that other factors such as gluon contributions may also play a significant role. Additionally, we observe that the proposed functions yield a collective flow component that closely matches the behavior of data from 5.02 TeV $p+Au$ collisions at large $k_\perp$. We also consider the possibility of gluon contributions to the proposed incoherent particle distribution function, and demonstrate that such contributions could result in significant effects on collective flow at mid and large angles. We conclude by outlining several potential experiments that could provide further insight into the proposed collective phenomena observed in small systems. Additionally, we suggest that the proposed $k_\perp$-dependent distribution functions may be relevant to large-time asymptotics and elliptic flow coefficient data from 5.02 TeV $p+p$ collisions at large $k_\perp$. We also outline several potential resolutions to the discrepancy between interacting quasiparticle model predictions and data from 5.02 TeV $p+Au$ collisions at large $k_\perp$. We conclude by considering the broader implications of the proposed $k_\perp$-dependent distribution functions on our understanding of collective behavior in quantum field theory

By leveraging both generative and classification tasks, our findings reveal that these models can infer relationships between entities even when there is no explicit language to do so. However, our data also highlights the presence of inaccuracies in these inferences, prompting us to introduce an innovative method to evaluate the performance of our model and other similar systems. This evaluation reveals that our approach surpasses the existing state of the art. Moreover, our data also sheds light on the limited ability of these models to accurately capture all the information present in a given text, a phenomenon we term as "information leakage." Despite this limitation, our results demonstrate the potential of these models to excel in a broader range of tasks that require reasoning about entities and their relationships. Our work also paves the way for further research into the ability of these models to reason about entities in complex contexts. Through a study of 83 galaxies with prominent radio emissions, it was found that those with limited magnetic fields in their accretion disks can exhibit gamma-rays in the high-energy spectrum.  In contrast, galaxies with restricted magnetic fields in their disks did not exhibit gamma-rays in the high-energy spectrum.  The findings suggest that disks contributing to gamma-rays must be involved in particle acceleration, consistent with theories of Active Galactic Nuclei, and that narrow-waisted disks are more capable of particle acceleration than broad-waisted disks.  It was also discovered that galaxies exhibiting gamma-rays have shorter black hole lifetimes and higher stellar velocities, and that the relationship between gamma-rays and narrow-waisted disks holds true across various black hole masses.  The study concludes that searching for narrow-waisted disks in Active Galactic Nuclei across the sky may lead to discovering new sources of gamma-rays.  Moreover, it was observed that the host galaxies of gamma-ray binaries feature narrow-waisted disks in 50% of the cases, in contrast to 10% of the control group, and that the relationship between gamma-rays and narrow-waisted disks in these galaxies is not solely dependent on the presence of an accretion disk.  Finally, it was suggested that in the process of forming a black hole, the environment surrounding the star may influence the formation of a disk, and that searching for narrow-waisted disks in the universe may provide valuable insights into the process of black hole formation.  It was also proposed that searching for narrow-waisted disks in the universe may be linked to the search for gamma-rays, and that the study's findings may have implications for the development of more sensitive detectors of such particles. Temporal sequence analysis typically relies on comprehensive training on lengthy sequences to extract meaningful information, but this limits our understanding of shorter sequences due to a lack of reference data. High-dimensional sequences also pose challenges because traditional methods usually analyze a single variable at a time, resulting in incomplete representation of complex biological processes that involve multiple variables and time. To overcome these obstacles, we propose an innovative approach called Guided learning of short and high-dimensional temporal sequences (GSHiTS) that allows for the analysis of shorter, high-dimensional temporal sequences. By leveraging existing knowledge from comprehensive training on longer sequences, GSHiTS effectively learns hidden patterns. We applied GSHiTS to an example involving the simultaneous measurement of gene expression in rice, where we analyzed temporal expression profiles for 46 genes across 128 time points with a sample of 25 profiles for each of five developmental stages. By incorporating information from longer expression profiles, we enhanced the identification of key regulatory modules and corresponding targets. Notably, we discovered previously unreported relationships between the clock gene PTL and other genes in rice. We address the recent anomalies observed in $K$ and $B$ meson decays, specifically focusing on possible explanations involving vectorlike doublets at an energy scale of $\sim 1$ TeV. Our analysis, conducted within the framework of the Standard Model, incorporates contributions from both the SM and new physics. Using profile likelihood methods for both individual and simultaneous analyses, we determined the most plausible values for the relevant input parameters $V_{ts}$ and $V_{td}$ along with the mass of the vectorlike doublet $m_D$. To classify musical instruments using audio from a new category that has not been seen before, we propose a method that leverages hierarchical connections between genres. Further analysis of our findings indicates that a substantial portion of accuracy gains can be attributed to the method's ability to mitigate biases in data, as evidenced by enhanced results on both easy and difficult tasks. Academic professionals typically rely on conventional literature searches to stay up-to-date with the latest research, but they often struggle to pinpoint specific knowledge gaps in their field. In contrast, modern artificial intelligence tools tend to utilize pre-trained models that are capable of extracting information from vast amounts of data, but these models often fall short when it comes to retrieving in-depth knowledge on a particular subject. In an attempt to bridge this gap, we've developed a unique dataset that contains questions aiming to retrieve new knowledge from existing research papers. Differing from conventional question-answering datasets that focus on factual retrieval, this dataset targets a deeper understanding of the subject matter. Additionally, we've incorporated several indicators to measure the quality of the retrieved knowledge and the diversity of the underlying research papers. With 5,000+ question-answer pairs spanning over 200 topics and incorporating a wide range of subjects such as biology, physics, chemistry, and social sciences, this dataset has the potential to serve as a benchmark to evaluate the ability of models to retrieve new knowledge from literature. We've also introduced three different evaluation metrics that correlate with human performance and have demonstrated improvements in the performance of state-of-the-art pre-trained models on this dataset. The code for these experiments can be found at https://github.com/ghulghule/knowledge-seeking and the dataset is available at https://github.com/ghulghule/knowledge-seeking/tree/main/dataset. We invite researchers to build upon this work by incorporating additional information from literature into knowledge-seeking questions. It comprises: a detailed manual guiding users through the construction process of suitable datasets, complete with data sets already integrated into the platform; a robust, user-friendly interface designed for user-driven acronym creation and management; the capacity for multiple interpretation methods; a secure, verifiable, and auditable process to ensure the validity of system evaluations; and comprehensive statistical analysis tools. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation environments and benchmark tasks. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge evaluation framework designed to assess the capabilities of reinforcement learning models in constant learning scenarios. L2Explorer leverages Randomized Dropout Neural Networks to generate an infinite variety of randomized levels for the existing 4D navigation task, known as MiniGrid, providing customizable policy space and control over difficulty levels. By combining multiple mini-tasks, L2Explorer enables the evaluation of lifelong learning policies in complex, dynamic environments. Its flexible design allows for the addition of additional evaluation metrics, custom learning protocols, and expanded suite of tasks to the existing randomized 4D navigation domain. To further advance research in lifelong learning, L2Explorer is an open-source, community-driven project, and we invite contributors to collaborate with us. By sharing their own implementations of continued learning methods and rigorous benchmarking of existing approaches, researchers and practitioners are also invited to join the L2Explorer community. Through our efforts, we aim to establish a unified framework for comparing the performance of state-of-the-art models and to drive innovation in the field of lifelong reinforcement learning. To get involved, please reach out to the L2Explorer team at https://github.com/UberTechnologies/L2Explorer. In response to changing needs and the development of more advanced evaluation methods, the framework's code will remain publicly accessible, along with the environment's source code at https://github.com/UberTechnologies/L2Explorer. In addition to its source code, the project will also be hosted on an official website with instructions for setting up the environment and example implementations of continued learning methods at https://www.uber.com/l2explorer. By providing a free, open-source evaluation environment for testing the capabilities of reinforcement learning models in real-world scenarios, we hope to contribute meaningfully to the field's advancement. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery, the process of creating process models from real processes to inform, monitor, and manage those processes. As processes involve multiple actors and produce vast amounts of data, discovering them requires advanced techniques and tools. While several methods for finding processes have been proposed, there's a lack of methods for identifying and eliminating process issues, such as deadlocks and cycles. This paper introduces a new approach to discovering processes using declarative models by analyzing data streams produced by the processes. It combines techniques from data stream processing, process data extraction, and model checking to create a method for declaring process properties and identifying process issues. This method is applied to a real-world process, a Java development process, and a web development process, showcasing its effectiveness. It also sparks ideas for enhancing process quality and detecting process problems. Furthermore, it highlights the need for a community-driven repository of process properties and a monitoring tool to check these properties. This allows for optimal recovery of hidden spatial mode information using maximum likelihood estimation, outperforming standard techniques. Furthermore, we find that this new detection methodology allows for resolution enhancement even when the resolution of the system is constrained by the Rayleigh criterion. Building on previous work by Maki, we explore the interplay between analytic and algebraic extensions in the moduli space $\mathcal{M}_{1,1}$. We demonstrate that a particular analytic extension can be formally expressed as an infinite product of algebraic extensions. This finding implies that the complex analytic structure on $\mathcal{M}_{1,1}$ is compatible with its algebraic structure. We also establish that the algebraic and analytic extensions share a common basis in terms of Teichm\"uller parameters. This common basis enables a clear expression of the algebraic and analytic properties of the monodromy action, as well as the cross-section of the branch cuts. Moreover, our results facilitate a precise description of the algebraic and analytic extensions of the Hilbert space and the harmonic map millimoduli space. These results are a significant contribution to the study of moduli spaces and their extensions. We hope this work will be of interest to the mathematics community. This study presents a novel, high-order numerical approach for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The developed method combines elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian schemes, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust algorithm capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A priori error analysis for the discrete problem is provided, demonstrating that the numerical solution converges to the exact solution at a rate of O(k^2 + h^4). Additionally, we demonstrate that our method is applicable to solving time-dependent mean field games systems, obtaining a conservative and consistent numerical solution. Notably, we establish that the limit of the discrete problem corresponds to the weak formulation of the continuous limit problem. A notable benefit of our approach is the generation of high-order accuracy for the macroscopic density at each given time, whereas existing methods typically yield first-order accuracy. This improvement is particularly significant in the context of mean field games, where the fractional order term presents an additional difficulty. We provide a concise analysis of our method and a detailed discussion of its implications for mean field games. Finally, we present a sample application, solving a mean field games problem with a bounded domain using both interior and boundary Nitsche penalties, demonstrating visually the accuracy of our results. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for spatially resolved, long-slit observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. Initial results show that for 7 of these galaxies, our data showed clear gas motions across multiple kiloparsecs. Furthermore, we discovered that 5 of these galaxies exhibit gas flows in the same direction as their stellar components, while 2 displayed counter-rotating gas motions. On the other end, we found that 3 of these galaxies showed gas motions significantly different from that of their stellar components, featuring both inner and outer regions with distinct rotation patterns. Additionally, we found that 4 of these galaxies exhibit linear extended gas motions, while 2 had curved gas motions and 1 had a combination of both linear and curved patterns. On the spectral front, we were able to detect both CO and Hα emissions in all of our target galaxies. Notably, we found higher CO-to-Hα ratios in the outer regions of 5 of these galaxies, and lower ratios in the inner regions of 4 of these galaxies. Our team plans to present more in-depth analyses, including comparisons with existing data and literature, in future presentations. We aim to explore the underlying causes of these variations, as well as their potential implications, through even more in-depth analyses. Ultimately, our observations will lay the groundwork for even more in-depth studies of gas motions in infrared galaxies using even more sensitive instruments on even more advanced telescopes in the future. High-resolution figures and additional context can be found in the appendix. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent in a single variable. By leveraging the properties of this new interpolation function, we design a piecewise quasi-interpolation operator that precisely conserves the shape of positive functions and generates non-negative values from non-negative data. The error bound of this operator is analyzed, and its computational efficiency is ensured by simple evaluation formulas. Several examples illustrate the operator's capability to preserve the shapes of polynomial, trigonometric, and exponential functions. Moreover, we demonstrate the operator's applicability in curve visualization using the example of the function $f(x,y) = \sin(x)\sin(y)$, and provide a comparative analysis of our method with respect to the classic linear operator. The implementation of this operator is also made available through a Python package called PyQuint. The benefits of this project include the preservation of shape information, improved aesthetic appeal, and the potential to support other visualization methods such as line integral convolution. Nevertheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper presents a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Our findings show that any two elements of V can be uniquely represented as reduced combinations of the generators, relying on a specific ordering of intervals that are equivalent to powers of the generator 'x'. This order is determined by the combinatorial structure of V's interval partial order, and we establish that the complexity of the word problem is directly linked to the depth of the highest interval combining the identities with powers of 'x'. Notably, we demonstrate that this depth is finite. A set is referred to as q-identifiable or p/q-identifiable for a given rational number p/q. The name q-identifiable originates from the work of J. Harvey and A. Menger. We aim to examine the characteristics of 1/q-identifiable sets when q exceeds 2, as well as the relationship between 1/q-identifiable and 1/p-identifiable sets for all rational numbers p and q where p > q. We also seek to determine the smallest universal integer N, where all 1/q-identifiable sets with q greater than N are equivalent to 1/p-identifiable sets for some rational number p, where p exceeds q. This problem initially arose within the context of distinguishing convex bodies using their x-ray functions. We utilize geometric arguments to analyze these sets and establish the desired results. Duality theory permits us to derive equivalent results for 1/p-identifiable sets with minimal alterations in the proofs. Notably, this result holds tangible value in the mentioned context of convex body classification. Last among our contributions, we explore the properties of 1/q-identifiable sets when q equals 1/2 or 2/3. For these instances, we identify the dual description of the corresponding polyhedron, referred to as P_2, but our findings do not provide insight into determining whether P_2 remains empty. We are confident that resolving this question would greatly contribute to both our results and those of Harvey and Menger. Consequently, our solutions can be applied to a broader context, encompassing a wider range of functions, such as affine functions or functions defined as the maximum or the sum of multiple linear functions. The concept of "shadow matter" originates from literature, referring to a hidden, world-like sector that interacts with our observable universe very lightly. Following this idea, we focus on a simple, axion-based world sector that contains a single extra neutrino flavor. Theoretical models involving this scenario are compatible with existing experimental data and do not introduce new challenges. In the context of dark energy cosmology, we found that this "axion-sterile-neutrino shadow matter" combination may take over the dark energy dominance near the present time, a phenomenon that could be confirmed through upcoming ice cube experiments at the South Pole. These experiments have the sensitivity to detect as little as one event per year across the 1000 cubic meters of ice targeted. Furthermore, we highlight that even if this event rate remains below the detection threshold, it would still imply a significant deviation from the standard neutrino background. In addition to providing a new perspective on the small-scale cosmological problem, we also offer a reason for the observed, anomalous arguments between large-scale and small-scale structure. Finally, we present several methods for detecting "axion-sterile-neutrino shadow matter" through astronomical observations, with the opportunity to explore its implications for the formation of galaxies and other celestial bodies. To this end, we also outline a new, multi-component extension of the standard model that incorporates sterile neutrinos and a right-handed Weyl fermion, for which we derive the most relevant low-energy processes and signal characteristics. With the advent of next-generation, sensitive astrophysical experiments, we are on the cusp of a breakthrough in determining whether "axion-sterile-neutrino shadow matter" constitutes a significant aspect of our universe's framework. In task-driven medical image analysis, pinning down specific objects or regions within images is a key challenge. This paper highlights the difficulties inherent in applying conventional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to extract meaningful region information, due to their fundamental design of scanning the entire image depth without differentiating between relevant and irrelevant volume. To overcome this limitation, this research introduces edge-gated CNNs, a novel architecture that allows specific information to be extracted from full image volumes. This design enables semantic partitioning of medical images, where objects are identified based on implicit region properties, such as density and texture. The proposed architecture is simple and easy to implement, and its effectiveness is demonstrated across multiple medical image datasets. The code for these examples is also publicly available for reproducibility purposes. This approach is particularly useful for medical image analysis, where accessing large amounts of labeled data is often difficult, and therefore, methods requiring only minimal labeled data are highly desirable. The paper explores the possibility of adapting this architecture to handle multiple objects, and several potential future directions are also identified. Despite its effectiveness, the edge-gated CNN still requires significant improvement, and several areas offer opportunities for innovation in medical computer vision. The edge-gated CNN is a simple yet powerful architecture that has only been applied to segmentation tasks, and research is needed to explore its potential in other medical computer vision tasks. We begin with a definition of executive function (EF) as a cognitive process that refines information through the elimination of irrelevant details, ultimately serving the purpose of making informed decisions. This process involves the reevaluation of previously held perceptions in light of new information, supported by a memory system that facilitates access to perished experiences. We leverage the concept of sequential decision-making to model EF by introducing a strategy that contrasts the value of alternative actions, thereby promoting a dynamic assessment of actions via hindsight learning. This approach results in a unified framework that addresses several key EF components, including planning, the management of internal states, and the refinement of internal representations. Through extensive simulation studies, our model demonstrates its capacity to tackle complex tasks, exhibit self-regulation, and refine its own cognitive processes. Moreover, the model's capacity to handle a diverse range of tasks is showcased through its application to multiple domains. We also introduce an innovative algorithm that illustrates the practical utility of our model in real-world scenarios. We hope that our work will contribute to a comprehensive understanding of EF and provide a foundation for further exploration of its underlying mechanisms. We invite other researchers to build upon our work and engage with our model through the open-source code available on GitHub. Leveraging multiple learning agents and a diverse range of tasks, we demonstrated that our model can successfully transition between various tasks and adapt to new situations. We also established a new benchmark for relational memory tasks and achieved state-of-the-art performance on multiple tasks. Through our study, we gained a deeper understanding of EF and developed a comprehensive model that integrates multiple cognitive components. We look forward to collaborating with other researchers and exploring further the underlying mechanisms of EF. Between 0.25 to 0.5 solar radii from the Sun's center, the solar wind slows and becomes densely packed due to particle interaction with solar breath, also known as the solar wind acceleration region. This study uses data from the Parker Solar Probe's flight in 2018 to 2020, where the spacecraft encountered this area on multiple occasions, and calculated the energy flux of the solar breeze as it entered the spacecraft's sensors. By applying a new mathematical filter that accounted for the effects of the solar wind's speed and density on the energy flux measurement, the energy flux of the solar breeze was found to be relatively consistent at around 2.4 watts per square meter when the solar wind's speed was 360 kilometers per second. This remained stable despite variations in the solar wind's speed and density, and no notable changes were found when the solar wind's speed increased to 600 kilometers per second. This implies that the solar breeze energy flux is determined by its speed and the distance from the Sun, and could have important applications in understanding the solar wind's behavior in the solar system. The data collected also provides valuable information on the solar wind's behavior during an solar flare, and further research is needed to analyze the data from the Parker Solar Probe's extended mission. This study was presented at the 31st meeting of the European Geophysical Union in 2020. A more detailed analysis of the data has been published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics in 2021. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under both ambient and high-pressure conditions.  Our X-ray diffraction data under pressure suggests that BFTO maintains its Aurivillius structure up to 2.5 GPa.  At higher pressures, above 4.5 GPa, a phase transition to a 2H-Nb$_2$O$_5$-type structure occurs, and this change persists as the pressure is reduced.  Our Raman spectroscopy results show that the phase transition is associated with the rotation of Bi$_2$O$_2$ layers, and this effect can be understood through band structure calculations.  Remarkably, our nuclear forward scattering measurements reveal an unexpected ferromagnetic state at room temperature under high pressure conditions, despite theoretical predictions of antiferromagnetic ordering.  This magnetic state persists upon pressure release, and is compatible with the 2H-Nb$_2$O$_5$-type structure.  We observe that this ferromagnetic state is not induced by the pressure itself, but rather by the phase transition, and is linked to the tilting of TiO$_8$ squares.  This discovery highlights the difficulty of predicting magnetic ground states in extrinsically compressed materials, and underscores the value of experimental investigation in this area.  Finally, we note that this material exhibits a unique combination of ferromagnetic ordering and low magnetic loss tangent, making it a promising candidate for high-frequency magnetic applications.  To utilize this material effectively, it is essential to understand the effects of compression on its structure and properties, and a detailed investigation of the high-pressure phase diagram of BFTO is therefore a priority.  In the course of this study, we determined the effects of various compression media on the structure and properties of BFTO, and have obtained evidence for a previously theoretical sensor application of this material.  This discovery has inspired plans to carry out a more comprehensive investigation of this property.  In the course of this study, we established the utility of Raman spectroscopy over X-ray diffraction in determining the structure of BFTO under high-pressure conditions, and have outlined the advantages of using resonant Raman over resonant X-ray scattering to probe the magnetic state of this material.  Lastly, we have demonstrated the value of combining experimental measurement, theoretical calculations, and material synthesis to advance our understanding of high-pressure phases in complex materials.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features on gigantic early-type galaxies using data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our study revealed that approximately 11% of 2649 massive early-type galaxies featured tidal structures exceeding 1% flux fraction. Observations showed these features generally had an elliptical shape with major axes ranging from 68 to 92 kpc. We discovered a clear correlation between tidal features and galaxy mergers, finding that galaxies with tidal features on their outskirts had a 1.5 to 2 times greater probability of being in the process of merging. This increase held for both minor and major mergers. Additionally, we found that the density of tidal features decreased as the distance from the galaxy's center increased, with features more common in the inner 40% of the galaxy's radius. This distribution held for both flat and dense galaxies. Our research further showed that galaxies with tidal features on their outskirts were rotating 1.3 to 1.5 times faster than those without such features. Our study provides a theoretical framework for identifying tidal features and sets the stage for a related study on the dynamics of galaxies with tidal features. That companion study will be presented in a separate paper. Our research suggests that the majority of gigantic early-type galaxies are not in a static state but are instead dynamic, interacting in the process of merging other galaxies. Our study will be combined with others to inform a larger study that will be a follow-up to that of Comerford et al. (2017).
