In our investigation, we observed that pre-trained language models perform inadequately when tasked with arranging words in a meaningful order, a skill that most people would find basic. To delve deeper, we selected the BART model and conducted a series of experiments to better understand its limitations. Our results reveal that BART's struggles stem from its difficulty in accurately identifying crucial words that help pin down the order, a problem we demonstrated by achieving substantial accuracy in a controlled experiment where the crucial words are clearly highlighted. Furthermore, we discovered that the performance drop is significant when words are randomly selected from a broader vocabulary, a decline that cannot be fully attributed to an increase in ambiguity. Our study provides valuable insights into the capabilities of pre-trained language models and highlights the need for more comprehensive evaluation frameworks that examine a model's ability to solve real-world problems that are often simplified in theoretical contexts. Our experiments are particularly relevant in this context, as they involve testing a model's capacity to solve a fundamental task that underlies many more complex applications, such as the generation of descriptive paragraphs. Our findings also emphasize the importance of collaborative evaluation across multiple research areas, as they highlight a discrepancy between the performance of BART on tasks like paragraph description tasks, which it excels at, and its lack of understanding for basic word arrangements that are essential for producing coherent descriptions. Our study concludes by emphasizing the need for more advanced methods that break down language models' performance into individual components and their interactions, as well as a call to action to the research community to address these methodological limitations and to collaborate across disciplines. Our work has been hosted on an open repository for reproducibility purposes, and we are eager to receive feedback from colleagues and to explore potential areas for further development. This feedback, along with our ongoing research, will be presented at a later date. Current studies examining the performance of random low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the receiver has full access to the transmitted bits, but in practice this is not always the case. To investigate the impact of degree discrepancies on LDPC code performance, we develop an iterative message-passing algorithm that accounts for the relationship between the degrees of the variable nodes and apply it to analyze the performance of LDPC ensembles over the binary deletion channel. By utilizing the degree-degree distribution and an extended density evolution approach, we demonstrate that this algorithm facilitates efficient transmission of degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles and evaluate its performance benefits for various degree distributions. Notably, our findings indicate that significant performance improvements can be achieved by incorporating degree-degree correlations, especially in scenarios with high erasure rates. Moreover, our results provide a framework for designing LDPC codes that incorporate degree-degree correlations and account for the specific characteristics of the channel they will operate over. This approach could lead to more efficient use of higher-density codes that would otherwise be too dense for certain channel conditions. Finally, we explore the application of this technique to other types of error-prone channels and show that it can be extended to tackle more complex scenarios. By utilizing higher-density codes that incorporate degree-degree correlations and adapting the density evolution approach, we believe we can further reduce the gap between theoretical bounds and real-world code performance. To that end, we propose an open problem of determining the maximum average degree of variable nodes that can be efficiently transmitted over the binary deletion channel. This threshold would serve as a benchmark for evaluating the efficacy of degree-degree correlated LDPC codes and guide future research in this area. Ultimately, our work contributes to the development of more efficient LDPC code designs that can accurately model real-world data patterns and provide a higher margin of error than traditional code performance benchmarks. As such, they have the potential to significantly improve the performance of data transmission over error-prone channels. Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves over algebraic number fields and finite fields. We also explore connections between the widths of inequalities and the counts of orders sharing the same set of minima widths. Finally, we offer a crystalline geometry interpretation to suggest that our findings may reflect underlying properties of geometric objects over algebraic varieties. We introduce a novel character representation, known as cluster character, for the representations of quantum groups. This character assignment leverages the inherent graph-theoretic structure of quantum groups, specifically their Iwama-Kashiwagi degenerations, to establish a direct connection between representations and cluster algebras. By building on existing work by Fock and Ginzburg, we demonstrate that degenerate irreducible representations correspond to extremal vertices in the quantum group's graph, enabling the computation of their cluster characters. Furthermore, we derive an explicit calculation method for the cluster characters of all representations. Moreover, we observe that the extremal vertex structure of degenerate irreducible representations yields distinct equalities among the cluster characters of all degenerate irreducible representations. Our framework allows us to introduce a non-degenerate generalization of the cluster character, which exhibits an intriguing connection to the classical character formula of Knop and Terras. Our results also imply a surprising, graph-theoretic characterization of degenerate representations in terms of their extremal vertex structure. Additionally, we demonstrate that the cluster character of a representation is solely determined by the representations' extremal vertices and their intertwining operators. Building on this understanding, we can further analyze the properties of the cluster character, including its behavior under involution and anti-involution actions, as well as its connection to the classical and spherical characters of quantum groups. Overall, our research enriches our knowledge of quantum groups, revealing their underlying structure and the fundamental nature of their representations. Moreover, our results suggest a broader theory of representation characterization based on graph-theoretic principles. This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with nuclear PDFs and temperature variations of the medium at start and end of the medium-probed jet formation process. Jet energy loss and medium-probed distance were varied to yield comparable jet energy in both simulations, allowing for a comparison of nuclear PDF effects, medium temperature effects, and their combination. Data from the LHC can be matched with simulated results using nuclear PDFs, while temperature variations have marginally notable effects on jet energy loss but significantly influence the tail of the jet $p_T$ distribution. News media frequently present balanced views, but sometimes also reflect the opinions of their publishers. To differenciate these scenarios, academics use various methods to measure news media polarization. Our analysis compares six recognized approaches to quantify polarization in news media and suggests a standard normalization process to ensure their compatibility. By normalizing the methods, we can effectively use techniques from multi-dimensional analysis to further investigate polarization in news media. Specifically, we apply a widely adopted approach, named IPS, and wrap it in our proposed normalization process. Our research reveals that normalization is crucial for accurate results, and we demonstrate our findings by analyzing the polarisation of 12 major news sources over a 4-year period. Our analysis indicates that some news sources exhibit stable polarisation patterns, while others exhibit polarisation that varies significantly over time. Our proposed framework is available online for others to use and reproduce our analysis at www.news-polarization.com. High-quality visual representations of our findings can be found at www.news-visuals.com. Our research also introduces a new method, named MDMA, which takes into account the polarising effect of external sources and provides a more comprehensive view of polarisation in news media. Our analysis of the 18 most popular news sources in the United States reveals that they exhibit polarisation patterns that vary significantly, with some consistent and others that changed over time. The ability to transmit solutions between layers is both facilitated and limited by the distinct connectivity patterns of each layer. As a result, various dynamic phenomena arise, such as synchronized states with partial information transfer, multiple unstable equilibrium points, and the mixing of local and global modes in multilayer networks with intermediate connectivity scales. The combination of analytical and numerical approaches used here can also be applied to multilayer networks with general type of variable evolution dynamics. Given a linear function that maps symmetric tensors to symmetric tensors, it can be reexpressed in a non-degenerate form using a unique transformation. This form has a specific parameterization that depends on the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the decomposition of the operator's defining matrix. Therefore, the number of parameters required to represent this operator is determined by the degeneracy of this matrix. A renowned decomposition formula due to Nanson's theorem essentially relates the operator's non-degenerate form to its original form and the material's second Piola-Kirchhoff stress. This connection allows for the recovery of the operator's parameterization by its original form, albeit possibly increasing the number of parameters. A new approach based on a decomposition formula adapted from Nanson's theorem provides a more efficient strategy when dealing with degenerate operators. This method utilizes eigenvectors associated with the operator's defining matrix and decomposes the relative rate of change of deformation into its components along these directions. By applying this strategy to each component, it is possible to obtain the operator's parameterization with a reduced number of parameters. This new approach facilitates a deeper understanding of an operator's parameterization by highlighting the physical significance of its parameters in terms of the material's response to distinct modes of deformation. Furthermore, this approach enables a broader classification of operators based on their parameterization. Researchers typically model complex networks as small-world networks, which possess a unique balance of local connectivity and short path lengths. Achieving accurate estimations of these properties is crucial for various applications including information dissemination and voting algorithms. In this work, a novel algorithm is developed to estimate network scales in small-world networks under the influence of malicious nodes. Unlike previous methods which rely on random walks or explicit node identifications, this algorithm leverages local information exchanges between neighbors. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations using real-world datasets, which show it can provide reliable scale estimations even in the presence of a significant proportion of malicious nodes. Notably, this algorithm offers better trade-offs in space and time complexity compared to existing solutions. Moreover, we outline a method by which this algorithm can be modified to estimate the network's diameter. This achievement is particularly significant as the development of this algorithmic solution resolved an open problem posed by Kempe and Tawrow in their paper 'On Detective Work' in 2003. The success of this algorithm paves the way for the further exploration of reliable algorithmic solutions in networks prone to malicious nodes. In numerical relativity, solving the Einstein field equations in conjunction with the constraint equations poses a challenge for the Conformal Flat Approximation (CFA) method in forming suitable spacetime metrics. To overcome this, our proposed approach modifies the strategy by explicitly resolving the constraint equations using a conformal thin-slice approximation, closely tied to the Combinatorial Total Variation diminishing (CTVK) method. We integrate an iterative solver for the conformal thin-slice equations and a unified scheme for the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints, both employing a preconditioned Conjugate Gradient algorithm. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by generating spacetime metrics for both vacuum and non-vacuum scenarios, including simulations of binary black hole mergers and stellar collapse leading to black hole formation with a prompt neutron star formation scenario. Our results show that our approach produces consistent outcomes and offers a more flexible framework for solving the Einstein equations. We also find that using a simpler approximation can result in misinterpreted physical phenomena, as evident in our simulation of a binary neutron star merger leading to black hole formation with a large deformation in spacetime. Overall, our approach provides a more robust solution to the Einstein equations and offers a deeper understanding of the role of spatial metric degrees of freedom in numerical relativity. We have made public our numerical codes based on the CTTK method, and we believe that this approach has the potential to enhance research in numerical relativity. We have also explored possible improvements, such as incorporating a better solver for the conformal thin-slice equations, and we anticipate that our approach will contribute positively to the advancement of numerical relativity in the future. Our paper detailing these results and code structure has been made available in the journal Classical and Quantum Gravity. We have further discussed our approach and our findings in a presentation at the 16th Conference of Numerical Relativity in China. This study presents the unusual Nernst effect in the Mn$_3$NiN film, an antiferromagnetic material with a small spin gap, whose heat transport mechanism is investigated through measurements of the transverse Nernst effect under an applied magnetic field. Our findings show that the anomalous Hall contribution dominates the unusual Nernst effect and that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is governed by the Caramete-Rao relation when the spin gap is minimal. However, an additional contribution beyond this relation becomes prevalent when the applied magnetic field exceeds the antiferromagnetic ordering field, likely caused by the transition of the quasiparticles to the spin gap region. This understanding holds implications for utilizing the unusual Nernst effect in magnetic materials for the detection of magnetic fields. This discovery may further enable the utilization of these materials in multi-terabit data storage technologies. The rise of big data in various sectors has led to an increased demand for deep neural networks that can efficiently process large quantities of information. However, training these neural networks is complex due to the high computational requirements, particularly the extensive memory needed by deeper networks. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel data distribution approach called Regional Critic Training, which leverages multiple GPUs through model-parallel learning to train neural networks efficiently. In this method, we divide the data into distinct regions and utilize a separate neural network for each region to calculate the gradient of the cost function. By doing so, we substantially reduce the memory required for training, as we only need to allocate memory for a single layer of the network. Systematically, we analyzed the optimal distribution of data regions in relation to network architecture, and our experiments involved a range of benchmark datasets across different application areas. Our results show that our approach not only facilitates the training of deeper networks on a single machine but also allows for easier implementation of distributed learning by following the model-parallel flow. Furthermore, we found that by optimizing the hyperparameters of the second neural network, we can effectively explore the balance between network depth and distribution without incurring significant costs. Our approach is particularly useful for areas where high-quality evaluation metrics are difficult to obtain, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on noisily labeled datasets by achieving accurate results with a small amount of additional training. Our code is available at https://github.com/hjdwng/region_critic. By building upon established algorithms and incorporating a new sampling strategy, we were able to enhance the performance of our model in multi-gpu training by a factor of five. Our research paves the way for further optimization of neural network training in resource-constrained environments. We have designed a novel control method that can be applied across multiple environments, utilizing limited and high-dimensional state space data, along with supplementary information from the system's dynamics. By combining a dynamic system identification technique and a novel representation of the system's dynamics, our approach creates a data-driven framework that can generate optimal controllers from the identified dynamics model. We demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by successfully teaching a robot to perform various tasks using only a compact set of data from the system's trajectory, along with additional information from the state space's boundary and a graphical representation of the system's dynamics. Notably, our approach excels over traditional reinforcement learning methods by requiring no trial-and-error learning and no reward signals. We also applied this approach to a complex aerodynamic system, predicting the occurrence of a vortex by analyzing the system's spatial features. By integrating this method with a vortex detection module, we successfully taught a drone to avoid vortex using only a compact data set and a simple spatial map of the system, highlighting the potential of this approach for handling complex and high-dimensionality systems. We also introduced an efficient algorithm for learning the system's identifier and demonstrated the approach's ability to handle noisy and limited data. We believe that this approach has significant implications for the control of complex systems across multiple domains and the development of safe and efficient policies for learning in dynamic environments. Quantum Ward identities, a key tool in studying conformal field theories (CFTs), are typically derived using correlation functions of primary fields. In this work, we develop an explicit approach to deriving Ward identities directly from the field theory's algebraic structure, using a combinatorial method inspired by the bootstrap hypothesis. Focusing on the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda CFT, we derive combinatorial formulas for the exponents and eigenvalues characterizing primary fields' transformation properties under the action of certain fields. By applying these identities, we can determine the coefficients of the conformal block decomposition of correlation functions involving the $\Phi$-fields, whose properties are not well documented. As a result, we obtain precise information about the conformal block structure, including the locations of branching points and poles, for both single and double correlation functions. This framework can be readily extended to other affine Toda CFTs. Notably, we find that the branching points in these theories exhibit a more intricate behavior than in minimal CFTs. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have paved the way for the development of sophisticated systems that enable users to achieve independence from debilitating paralysis. However, there is still a significant gap in translating existing BCI technology into a viable treatment for the high number of patients struggling with motor impairments caused by conditions such as spinal cord injuries and stroke. One promising approach to bridge this disparity is the incorporation of machine learning-based methods in low-density electrical recordings from the cerebral cortex. However, a major limitation in these systems has been the requirement for extensive training sessions to effectively operate the BCI, thereby rendering them unsuitable for individuals with limited mobility. Furthermore, these users often have limited access to sophisticated recording equipment due to its bulkiness and the need for a highly trained medical team to set it up. Advances in portable and cost-effective technologies such as wearable inertial sensors and mobile apps have created new opportunities for developing simpler, more user-friendly BCI systems that are easier to implement and require less training. One such system involves monitoring the individual's gait to control a smartphone-based BCI through various step-based commands, such as mail composition and sending an email. However, there are concerns regarding the effectiveness of these systems due to their reliance on pre-defined algorithms that are based on limited data from only a few subjects. Identifying leading drivers of changes in time series is crucial for data analysis, particularly when working with high-frequency data sets of varying dimensions. A prominent approach, Granger causality, has been extensively applied but holds limitations in complex systems due to its restrictive assumptions. We developed a novel causal discovery method tailored for time series data that circumvents these issues and allows for discovery of causality across different frequencies. This new approach builds upon VanderWalle's connectivity estimation framework and Generalized Phase Locking Value to efficiently uncover bidirectional and directional causal connections between non-linear time series variables. To enhance scalability, we introduced a new dimensionality reduction technique and successfully validated our framework on a range of synthetic and real-world datasets, including electroencephalogram recordings. Our results demonstrate its capacity to recover known causal relationships and outperform leading alternatives. We openly share our algorithm's code and an user-friendly interface is available for public use. Despite achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods, our model boasts significantly fewer parameters than alternative neural networks, facilitating its seamless integration into ensemble learning. We explore this capability with a subset of brain recordings, highlighting our framework's potential to enhance complex systems estimation. Finally, we outline possible extensions to our method and provide a framework for testing alternative dimensionality reduction techniques. We also examine the representational difficulty of the dataset, suggesting some datasets may not yield a clear low-dimensional representation. We anticipate our framework to contribute positively to the machine learning community. We await future opportunities to collaborate with other researchers. Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators, including single-event tools like the break-point model and the binary tree-decomposable model, as well as multi-event tools such as the distribution model and the binary and general reticulate model. By utilizing summary statistics such as likelihood ratios, entropy measures, and network statistics, we evaluate and contrast the capabilities of these methods across different parameter settings, scenario types, and network sizes. Our study comprises 13 different generators and 7 types of networks and covers a wide range of combinations of reticulate events. Our findings are our primary contribution, and they will guide researchers in selecting the most suitable network generator for their specific applications. Ultimately, this study paves the way for further investigation into the properties and behavior of phylogenetic network generators. To facilitate replication and the exploration of additional generators, our methodology is freely available for download at https://github.com/ComparingNetworkGenerators/ComparingNetworkGenerators. To assist users in selecting the most appropriate generator for their needs, we have devised a practical guide that can be accessed at https://ComparingNetworkGenerators.github.io/main/. This study is an initiative of the Phyloinformatics Hub, and we invite all researchers who work with phylogenetic networks to collaborate with us. This paper explores the phenomenological implications of a natural, complex MSSM framework that generates the Higgs mass naturally. Focusing on the effects of complex parameters, we have found the following key observations: Firstly, compared to the real parameter case, natural parameter choices lead to larger corrections from SUSY loops to the Higgs boson's couplings with a significant impact on its decay into bottom quarks. Secondly, natural choices of parameters that involve the complex Abelian gauge sector can cause the CP-violating part of the Higgs self-interaction to be naturally large, resulting in an enhanced decay into bottom and anti-bottom quarks. Furthermore, we have found that the CP-violating part of the lightest neutral Higgs boson's self-interaction is naturally large when natural parameter choices are made, leading to an enhanced decay into bottom and anti-bottom quarks. Consequently, this implies an increased sensitivity to the CP-violating phase of the top quark's left-handed singlet pole mass in the lightest neutral Higgs boson's decay. A key concept in time series analysis is the partial linear model, which combines the strengths of linear regression and additive models. While testing for linearity is a well-defined problem in traditional autoregressive models, the introduction of non-linear components using the natural anchor approach makes interpretation more complex in time series cross-section models. In particular, the presence of non-linear terms can confound the estimation of parametric components, potentially leading to inefficient estimation and biased inference. To address this issue, we develop a new testing framework for linearity that accounts for non-parametric network effects and allows for the identification of linearity within specific networks. Notably, our approach surpasses the limitations of existing tests by accommodating time-varying connections and complex non-linear interactions. Our theoretical findings include a central limit theorem for the test statistic under the true linearity scenario, as well as a uniform boundary theorem that provides a justification for our test's critical values. Our results are corroborated by simulations, and a real-world application involving GDP data highlights the efficacy of our linearity test. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in blockchain technology has made it an appealing platform for building various applications, however the same features that guarantee network security also create difficulties in detecting illicit activities. While numerous studies have been conducted to identify hackers by tracking their addresses, our research expands on this effort by examining the currency trails left by perpetrators with limited resources. Utilizing a comprehensive dataset of 114,807 addresses derived from the Ethereum blockchain and associated smart contract code, our study reveals that suspicious actors display distinct behavior in terms of currency trails. Contrary to common wisdom, our findings indicate that malicious actors tend to maintain a more manageable number of active addresses, rather than the maximum possible. Additionally, our research reveals that the address selection strategy employed by these actors follows a mix of both exploratory and greedy patterns. A notable consequence of this behavior is the creation of distinct clusters within the blockchain graph, specifically in the small-world component. Our study also delves into the area of machine learning, although the current classification techniques are not advanced enough to differentiate between good and bad actors based on currency trails alone. Nevertheless, our research lays the groundwork for further exploration of these findings and the development of more sophisticated methods for identifying harmful behavior within the blockchain. This study introduces a novel integration approach for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional methods can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration method aims to overcome this limitation by distinguishing between two time steps: a shorter time step for flow simulations and a longer time step for particle collisions. Our method integrates the collision map into a semi-implicit method and integrates the flow simulation using an explicit method. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's essential to incorporate a wide range of semantic relationships into the question-answering process. Current advances in CQADuo tasks primarily focus on sophisticated multi-step processes, intricate world knowledge, and diverse semantic connections. However, it's crucial to acknowledge that not all such questions demand the same level of complexity. To make progress in this domain, it's necessary to categorize CQADuo questions based on their inherent difficulty levels and underlying semantic relationships. In this work, we introduce a novel framework known as Coarse-to-Careful (C2C) that achieves this task. The C2C framework consists of two key components: a coarse-level model that identifies primary semantic connections among questions and generates initial answers through a single-step process; a careful model that refines the understanding of semantic connections among questions and generates more accurate answers through a multi-step process. The framework introduces a new set of challenging follow-up questions designed to test its effectiveness. On the CQADuo benchmark, the C2C framework demonstrates superior performance when compared to baseline models, consistently outperforming them by over 5% in overall score. In addition, a new set of challenging follow-up questions opens up possibilities for pre-trained models to be evaluated on their ability to effectively utilize world knowledge. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for complex signal processing. Furthermore, we explored various applications of this technology in an attempt to overcome several challenges faced by traditional spectroscopy, notably distorting template spectra and inaccurate device calibration. Ultimately, we successfully employed this technique to measure the Doppler shift in a moving light source and accurately calibrate our photonic device using reference lights with known spectral profiles; our findings suggest the potential for photonic devices to be integral in various astrophotonic applications. Detailed instructions on fabricating these photonic devices and performing experiments with them are included in this paper. We believe that the principles of photonic technology in combination with our findings could pave the way for a new generation of low-cost, portable, and highly sensitive photonic devices capable of performing cross-correlation techniques on a variety of parameters, thus making them an exciting development in the field of astrophotony. Furthermore, the unique features of these photonic devices could also be incorporated into traditional spectroscopy to enhance its performance. We hope that this work will spark a renewed interest in the field of astrophotony and the development of a new generation of low-cost, portable, and highly sensitive photonic devices. In the current landscape of cross-device federated learning, participating devices typically follow a client-server framework, where they connect to a central server that updates model parameters. This approach has significant connectivity drawbacks, particularly when dealing with a vast number of devices with limited connectivity to the server. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel random walk approach, enabling self-learning in cross-device federated learning settings. This method allows devices to collaborate with neighboring devices without needing connectivity to the server, thereby expanding their knowledge of the data distribution. We develop a random walk-based algorithm that leverages local optimization and client-server updates, and analyze its performance in heterogeneous settings. Our results show that this self-learning approach leads to faster convergence and improved model accuracy compared to traditional client-server frameworks. We also demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through experiments and real-world applications. Notably, we successfully applied our method to a large-scale taxi routing scenario in New York City. Knowledge tracing has emerged as a prominent field in recent years to develop intelligent adaptive learning systems. A subset of knowledge tracing focused on student knowledge assessment uses log data from interactive learning platforms, known as online knowledge tracing. We have observed significant progress in the field with the application of deep learning techniques, yet a limitation exists in the form of unavailability of open-source tools to test knowledge tracing models. To address this gap, we present pyKT, a Python-based library that provides data preprocessing capabilities, utility functions for model evaluation, and a command-line interface for user interactions. By utilizing popular deep learning and data preprocessing libraries such as PyTorch and TensorFlow, along with common machine learning tools like Scikit-learn, pyKT enables researchers and practitioners to easily evaluate their own knowledge tracing models. The library's versatility allows it to handle a wide range of deep learning-based models and common data preprocessing techniques commonly used in online knowledge tracing tasks. Furthermore, pyKT includes a user-friendly command-line interface that facilitates quick model testing, enabling users to focus on the development of innovative knowledge tracing models. With the release of this open-source library, we contribute to the advancement of the knowledge tracing community by providing a free resource for testing deep learning-based models. In conjunction with this library, we also introduce a new publicly accessible dataset called the "EDX Dataset," derived from edX course interactions. This new dataset, combined with the pyKT library, is an important step forward in the development of adaptive learning systems. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of pyKT through the evaluation of multiple deep learning-based knowledge tracing models, including the application of attention mechanisms and graph neural networks. This work represents an important contribution to the knowledge tracing community, with the EDX Dataset and the pyKT library available for download on the project website. With the continuous enhancement of feature engineering and model architecture innovation, we anticipate even greater advancements in the field of knowledge tracing. As such, we invite the broader research community to collaborate with us and contribute to the further development of this field. In particular, we encourage practitioners to test their own knowledge tracing models using the provided code and the EDX Dataset, with all experimental results expected to be reproducible. In exchange for using this open-source library, we kindly request that users cite this work in their published findings. In conclusion, we have established a solid foundation for the development of adaptive learning systems with the release of pyKT and the EDX Dataset, and we look forward to working together with the research community to drive innovation in this exciting field. Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT was the winner in all tracks using the SMT-LIB2 format, which was introduced just a year prior. Since then, SMT solvers have evolved significantly, with many developing sophisticated strategies and techniques to solve complex formulas. To better understand this progress, we surveyed the most recent edition of the SMT-COMP competition held in 2021, where 37 participating solvers were evaluated against each other using over 17,000 benchmarks in various categories. Our analysis revealed several key observations: first, no single strategy proved effective across all types of problems; second, many solvers combined different approaches to achieve best results; third, solving times for many benchmarks still far exceed what is acceptable for practical applications. Against this backdrop, our project aims to provide a unified framework for expressing formulas and proofs that can be used to inform the development of more efficient and diverse SMT solvers. Our proposed format, which we call Alethe, is an extension of the widely adopted SMT-LIB2 format, with additional features such as flexible theorem scheme support and a novel proof representation based on sorted connections between formulas and strategies. To showcase the potential of Alethe, we created a version of the SMT-COMP competition benchmarks that use our proposed format and obtained superior results by a state-of-the-art solver using Alethe-formatted input, which we found surprising given our understanding of the underlying techniques used by modern solvers. Our project is an open effort to gather feedback and insights from the research community, and we invite all interested parties to share their thoughts and contribute to further developments. Our proposed format and associated tools are already available for exploration and testing. In addition to format improvements based on user feedback, our plan includes the organization of a competition for solving Alethe-formatted formulas as a legacy of the original goal that motivated this project and to create a benchmark suite that can be used to evaluate the performance of state-of-the-art SMT solvers. Our objective is to ensure that future developments in our proposed format reflect the expertise and knowledge of the broader research community. However, the internal structure of these rafts remains poorly understood due to their irregular shape and the need for high-resolution 3D imaging to observe them properly. Previous models attempting to describe this structure are based on simplified representations of cell behavior that are now being replaced by a more comprehensive framework that takes into account the intricate details of cell adhesion forces. A new method for precision measurement is introduced and used to study the structure and cell migration patterns in three different types of large cell aggregates. Furthermore, ANs require significantly fewer parameters than their equivalent parameter count, achieving this with a relatively simple architecture and no optimization techniques. We take on the problem of hyperedge identification, which involves using a training set to build a model that predicts undirected graphs representing specific protein interactions based on their genetic characteristics and the locations of their genes. By assuming that the training graphs are actually undirected graphs wrapping up interacting hyperedges, we develop a novel algorithm that uses this model to accurately reconstruct the hyperedges from the training graphs. We also explore ways to extend this method to larger datasets and more complex situations.

In our research, we address the challenge of learning from experienced agents in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning. By assuming that the agents' current policies are safe and effective, we develop a computational method to create a new policy that combines their benefits. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to collaborative multi-agent scenarios in random environments and complex video game environments. This phenomenon is particularly pronounced in fields like physics, where the rate of new discovery slows with each passing year. In contrast, fields like biology experience a rapid expansion of new knowledge without a corresponding decrease in productivity. To gain insights into these differences, our analysis incorporates metrics such as productivity, knowledge amount, and a newly defined disparity metric. As a consequence, we derive conditions for a one-dimensional ring to be F-regular, involving its total ring dimension and the coefficients of its Hilbert function. Building on these results, we explore the relationship between F-regularity and the total ring dimension in dimensions greater than one. Notably, we identify a one-dimensional component in a higher-dimensional ring that must share certain properties with its prime ideal components. Specifically, we found that the total ring dimension is equal to the maximum of all one-dimensional components plus the number of prime ideal components. This insight enables us to conclude that a one-dimensional ring is F-regular if and only if its total ring dimension is one. For higher-dimensional rings, we discovered that the total ring dimension must be equal to the sum of all one-dimensional components. As a result, we determined that in a d-dimensional ring, the total ring dimension can range from d to d+1. Finally, we demonstrate that there exist infinite families of F-regular d-dimensional local rings for total ring dimensions of both d and d+1. We investigate the potential of future $e^+e^-$ colliders to shed light on theories that include additional scalar fields beyond the standard model, primarily focusing on a minimal extended scalar sector with one additional scalar field. In this context, we comprehensively analyze the production process of a $Z$ boson and a Higgs boson at a next-generation $e^+e^-$ collider, specifically when the Higgs boson decays into photons. Our thorough assessment accounts for both an ideal detector system and the design parameters of the CEPC, FCC-ee, and CLIC, and reveals that in the most optimistic scenario, a one-standard-deviation sensitivity can be achieved for a mass scale of around $3.2$ TeV. High-energy particles with masses beyond the TeV range are difficult to confirm through traditional means due to their limited interaction with matter. If we assume these particles are also short-lived, as is common in many theoretical models, then their existence would lead to observable signatures in the cosmic string spectrum. Specifically, if these particles have lifetimes shorter than 10-16 seconds, then their effect would be evident in the form of cut-offs or patterns in the cosmic string's gravitational wave frequency spectrum. This constraint could further lead to limits on the production of these particles at high-energy collisions, potentially influencing existing experimental sensitivity thresholds. For example, the LHC could potentially detect particles with masses up to 100 TeV if their existence is supported by evidence from cosmic string research. This connection allows us to reconcile the apparent discrepancy between the lack of direct evidence for new physical phenomena at the LHC and the limitations of existing constraints from other indirect methods, such as cosmic microwave background observations. As such, we introduce a new criterion for evaluating the discovery potential of existing and future experiments, including the ability to probe new physics through its potential to leave secure or insecure signatures in natural or man-made environments. As a result, we expect future experiments to focus not only on improving existing limits on secure new physics but also on detecting new physics that could be insecure, even if it means revising existing experimental sensitivity thresholds. Moreover, we emphasize that existing and near-future experiments have significant capabilities in detecting new physics that could be insecure, including heavy particles with masses up to EeV range, in various natural and man-made environments that could serve as targets for further astrophysical and cosmological investigations. We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to
simulate competition among firms, seeking to determine if their application can
yield a stable Nash Equilibrium. Our results indicate that these algorithms
effectively facilitate firms' discovery of optimal production levels, with some
variants exhibiting exceptional speed and accuracy in reaching a Nash Equilibrium.
To further validate our findings, we conducted multiple tests, including: 
* Comparing the performance of different algorithm components to see if they
  contribute to reaching a Nash Equilibrium;
* Examining whether the obtained results are firm-specific or dependent on the
  particular population used in the game;
* Observing the behavior of the firms when the algorithm is interrupted and the
  search space is limited;
* Applying the algorithm to a broader sample of Cournot games with an added
  third firm;
* Analyzing the performance of the algorithm when the firms' search capabilities
  are limited. 
Our research provides initial evidence that co-evolutionary genetic algorithms can
effectively facilitate firms' search for a Nash Equilibrium in a manner
consistent with theoretical models. Moreover, these algorithms demonstrate a high
degree of search efficiency, with some variants yielding results that align with
predictions made by models that incorporate search costs. Our results are of
greater significance as they suggest that models incorporating search costs
and stochastic firm behavior can yield similar results with a simpler model. We
believe our research will be useful to researchers exploring the application of
co-evolutionary genetic algorithms to similar games and models. 
We invite feedback from these researchers and are open to sharing our data and
model specifications in detail. Our results offer insights that can be applied to
theoretical models, while our data could facilitate the development of new models
that explore different variants of the Cournot game. 
Furthermore, our research could provide a framework for investigating other markets
and games by promoting a more nuanced approach to defining and measuring the
Nash Equilibrium in games involving search costs. 
Our research could also offer a new perspective to economists working on dynamic
models and stochastic firm behavior, as well as those exploring the application
of genetic algorithms and machine learning in an economic context. 
We anticipate that our research will be of greater interest to economists with a
background in computational modeling and machine learning, particularly those with
an interest in computational economics, genetic algorithms, and machine learning.

Recent studies using observational data have shown that using a single template to fit the spectral energy distribution (SED) of galaxies leads to an overestimation of star formation rates (SFRs). To resolve this issue, using multiple templates or latent variable models has been proposed to address this limitation. In this study, we examine the relationship between different SED models' estimates of SFR and the observed Brackett-$\gamma$ emission. It is observed that the traditional single-template SED models overestimate SFRs in low-mass galaxies, while in high-mass galaxies, the best-fitting temperatures from using multiple SED templates or latent variable models are actually lower than those determined through Brackett-$\gamma$ diagnostics. Furthermore, when comparing the two methods, we find a scatter of $\sigma_{\rm ratio} = 0.24$ in the ratio of SFRs to Brackett-$\gamma$ luminosities, indicating an overall good agreement but with significant deviations. Given that Brackett-$\gamma$ is less affected by dust than ultraviolet continuum, it is considered a reliable standard for evaluating SFRs. Therefore, rather than modifying the physical parameters of SED models, we propose using the ratio of observed Brackett-$\gamma$ luminosities as a gold-standard to evaluate the performance of different SED models and their variants. This evaluation shows that using two-component SED models or latent variable models with a Gaussian Process prior results in the most accurate performance, while using single-template SED models or a Bayesian model with a uniform prior for the stellar mass leads to the least accurate results. Moreover, we find that incorporating an active gravitational lensing signal does not significantly improve the agreement between observed and predicted Brackett-$\gamma$ luminosities. Finally, we explore how to apply this evaluation method to evaluate the performance of different gas mass estimators. Mobile agents require efficient and reliable localization systems that rely on internal state rather than external infrastructure. By integrating visual and inertial sensors, this technology offers location determination and trajectory tracking. However, the inherent noise in inertial measurements and the limited field of view of cameras poses a significant challenge. To address this, we present an innovative method called EMA-VIO, utilizing an external memory attention mechanism to augment the recurrent state estimator with environmental information extracted from monocular visual data. This results in a highly efficient and lightweight system that provides precise location tracking even in complex scenarios. Our experiments demonstrate EMA-VIO's superiority over existing VIO methods with reduced drift and accuracy improvements of up to 61% in challenging scenarios. Furthermore, our research shows that external memory attention boosts the system's ability to recover from synchronization errors, resulting in a significant reduction in mean localization errors. Additionally, we highlight the applicability of this technology to mobile robots by successfully integrating the system with a wheel encoder and demonstrating its effectiveness in tracking the robot's trajectory. Comprehensive experiments, conducted in real-world scenarios with varying lighting conditions and weather, showcase the robustness and reliability of EMA-VIO. To facilitate replication, we publicly release all experimental data, configuration files, and source code for the EMA-VIO framework. Approximately twenty years ago, a theoretical framework consisting of grid cells in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) was proposed. This framework, first introduced by Hasselmo and his colleagues, suggests that grid cells' unique spatial patterns of activity could provide a scalable system for navigating complex environments. Subsequent research has remarkably confirmed many predictions associated with this framework, resulting in extensive studies on grid cells from various perspectives. This paper aims to provide an informative survey of the existing body of research related to grid cells, covering key findings and notable research contributions. Furthermore, it highlights several intriguing questions that remain unanswered and invites fellow researchers to contribute to this field. Additionally, associated open-source code and a user-friendly database of grid cell data are made available for public use. In conclusion, this survey reiterates the significance of further investigating the grid cell network to uncover vital insights into our brain's neural mechanisms. As such, it encourages multidisciplinary research that integrates theoretical models, computational models, and experimental approaches to study this network's dynamics and function. Unaddressed questions posed in this survey's context of the hippocampal subsystem pose challenges for brain navigation that remains an unresolved issue for modern robots. Therefore, it is essential to acknowledge the contributions of all researchers who have contributed to the understanding of grid cells and looks forward to their continued contributions in the future. Throughout a solar-type main sequence star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, influencing its global magnetic activity. As the star ages, its rotational velocity slows, passing through several distinct phases characterized by distinct differential rotation patterns. In the rapid-rotation phase, the star's rotation is too swift for stellar convection to influence its rotational velocity. Once rotation speeds slow to a point where convective turbulence can impact the star's internal dynamics, the impact of anti-solar differential rotation on the dynamo process becomes evident. Using three-dimensional global simulations of solar-type stars, this study examines the influence of anti-solar differential rotation on their dynamos throughout their main sequence lifetime. It demonstrates how a reduction in rotational velocity below a certain threshold, where convective turbulence starts to impact the star's internal dynamics, leads to a reversal in the $\alpha$-effect's symmetry. This shift in $\alpha$-effect symmetry occurs over a wide range of rotational velocities and doesn't significantly impact the strength of the differential rotation. In the semi-convection zone, a change in the solar-type star's rotation velocity causes a switch in the sign of the $\alpha$-effect, resulting in a reversal of the toroidal magnetic field's generation. This, in turn, leads to a cyclic behavior driven by the star's slow rotation in the quasi-convective regime. It also enables a possibility of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating solar-type stars. This scenario is expected to occur commonly as many stars spend a significant amount of time in the quasi-convective regime during their main sequence lifetime. This process may also contribute a large fraction of magnetic energy observed in slowly rotating stars. It also produces large-scale magnetic field structures like stars with the largest magnetic field strengths, like the Ap stars. This requires a revision of previous models that only considered rapid rotation and produced short-winded cycles. It also implies that the operation of $\alpha^2$-dynamos might extend to a broader range of rotational velocities than previously assumed. It also suggests re-evaluating the requirements for a dynamo's existence in solar-type stars with low rotation rates. Ion emission from droplets, especially those made of a hygroscopic substance like glycerol, has been extensively used in various applications including particle surface characterization and to generate ions for mass spectrometry. Yet, the underlying process of ion generation through the interaction of a laser with these droplets remains poorly understood. We address this knowledge gap by employing super-resolution imaging, or reaction nanoscopy, in conjunction with droplet lasers. Our study shows that the formation of ions results from the interaction between a plasma and the droplet's surface rather than volume. Furthermore, we observe the creation of micro-jets, which we believe are responsible for the appearance of plasma patterns seen under an optical microscope. We also find that the droplet's surface curvature influences the migration of ions. Our key contributions include the integration of reaction nanoscopy and droplet lasers, as well as a droplet model that accounts for both its internal and external effects. One key challenge in this field is developing a scalable and comprehensive framework that integrates tissue hierarchies for actionable insights.  Inspired by the potential of hierarchical network representations to model complex biological relationships,  we explore their application in cancer gradient prediction by developing a multi-level graph neural network called CancerHIN.  CancerHIN learns from expert-annotated histopathology images with spatial relationships between cancer cells and the surrounding tissue by learning from multiple levels of histological organization.  By integrating the learned representations from each level,  CancerHIN effectively identifies key tissue patterns that are indicative of cancer progression.  Experimental results show that our proposed framework achieves superior cancer gradient prediction performance when compared to state-of-the-art methods.  Additionally,  we highlight the potential of CancerHIN to provide valuable insights for oncologists that can be used to develop patient-specific treatment plans.  By leveraging the capabilities of hierarchical network representations,  we believe that our approach lays the groundwork for breaking down cancer barriers through the detection and analysis of tissue architecture. Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters or online messages, are used extensively in various studies. A key point process model for such applications is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which can exhibit persistent behavior and calculate the long-term expected rate of events. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian method for estimating the Hawkes process model, including its nonlinear components. Although Bayesian estimation is generally preferred for its comprehensive uncertainty measures, the nonparametric Bayesian approach is essential due to the limited availability of nonlinear Hawkes process posteriors. To address this challenge, we first derive the exact conditional distribution of the nonlinear Hawkes process given past event data. Although this conditional distribution does not have a recognizable form, we can still employ Monte Carlo methods to simulate from it. In particular, we discuss the advantages and limitations of two main approaches: the independent sample approximation and the importance sampling approximation. By examining the theoretical properties of the proposed methods, we establish the conditions under which they produce accurate results. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods, we present results from various experiments, including synthetic data sets and an analysis of real-world event data. Our results show that the proposed methods can provide more precise estimates than classical maximum likelihood estimation and are robust to persistent processes. Additionally, we find that the methods can handle missing data and offer uncertainty quantification. Notably, our results indicate that the independent sample approximation can be scaled up for complex data sets, while the importance sampling approximation is more efficient but requires more careful tuning. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in decreasing this burden, but they are hindered in complex datasets by a limited number of labeled samples. One method to enhance performance involves leveraging existing annotations from similar anatomical structures with readily available labeled data, even if those structures are not identically the same. Nevertheless, this approach is challenged by the need to account for variations in patient data, different imaging modalities, and expert-provided inconsistent segmentations. To tackle this issue, we propose Contrastive Semi-Supervised Learning (CSL), a method that employs a contrastive learning approach to take advantage of the existing annotations from comparable anatomical structures, even in the presence of noisy labels. CSL is designed to adapt to multiple anatomical structures and is suitable for a variety of deep learning frameworks, including Multi-task Learning (MTL) and Self-supervised pre-training. The proposed method is employed to achieve domain adaptation in segmenting comparable cross-anatomical structures across different organs, providing superior performance when compared to control experiments and established methods. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a configuration using LE arrays. By combining multiple LE modules with aligned fields of view, this design aims to achieve a broader observational area while maintaining high pixel densities. With eight LE modules, a prototype has been developed that boasts ~1.4 steradians of coverage and 36,000 pixels at ~3.5 arcseconds per LE unit. Initially prototyped for optical detection, the design is now being adapted for X-ray usage with the development of high-density, low-noise image sensors. This prototype has the capability to transition between full frames and a data-driven, LE-specific readout mode. The prototype's effectiveness will be validated through laboratory testing and a later astronomical observation with the prototype. This innovative design is poised to significantly impact future X-ray optics development by demonstrating the viability of large-format LE detectors in wide-field monitors. This includes large-area coverage with high pixel densities, making-in-volume (MIV) manufacturing feasible. This design is part of a broader research effort to explore novel lens designs and their applications across multiple wavelengths. While LE optics are well-suited for applications requiring high pixel densities, such as real-time optical monitoring or planet detection. For astronomical use, however, LE optics are generally used in a non-resolving mode, resembling the configuration of a re-binned CCD. Consequently, in such scenarios, the unique benefits of LE optics over other wide-field optics, such as the effective area and point-spread function, often justify the increased pixel coverage. This prototype has implications for the development of large-area, low mass X-ray detectors, such as those employing LE-shaped micro-calorimeter arrays. This could potentially improve the sensitivity of X-ray telescopes in the 0.5-7.5 keV band by up to a factor of ~13 over the current best-in-class detector technology. This development is also relevant to the X-ray telescope currently being designed as part of the (e)ASTRO mission, a partnership between the University of Oulu, the University of Turku, the University of Helsinki, the Aalto University, the Finnish Space Agency, and the NASA. This prototype has also shown that LE optics can effectively be used as a monitoring tool to catch the maximum flux or the critical phase of a transient object. Converting ancient music notes into audible sound is a challenging Music Information Retrieval (MIR) task, primarily due to a lack of well-organized data. One key step in this process involves automatically transcribing keyboard recordings, which can be accomplished by a technique called Source Separation. In this study, we propose a semi-supervised Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (CNMF) method to execute this task. This approach builds upon the established multilinear factorization model and adapts it for processing continuous audio recordings represented as 3D matrices. By incorporating a constrained optimization process and an alternative update rule, our model surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques, including both supervised and unsupervised methods. We also utilize a novel initialization strategy to enhance the model's performance in real-world applications. Notably, our approach has the unique benefit of processing recordings that include multiple overlapping sounds. We initiate evaluations using a newly collected and publicly accessible dataset comprising seven hours of recorded organ music with accurate transcriptions. Our results show significant improvement over existing methods, with an overall accuracy of 84.5%. This represents a notable increase from the previous state-of-the-art technique and confirms the effectiveness of CNMF for this specific task. However, CNMF's performance still declines when applied to recordings featuring piano music, indicating a potential need for further optimization. Ultimately, our proposed approach holds promise for the development of more sophisticated music retrieval tools. To facilitate this progress, we release an improved version of the publicly accessible dataset containing additional piano recordings with accurate transcriptions. This dataset, now comprising over 5 hours of recorded organ and piano music, is available for download at the provided URL. By initiating evaluations using this dataset and a newly introduced evaluation metric called Mean Ranks, we hope to contribute to the development of more robust music retrieval methods. Furthermore, we plan to build upon these experiments by exploring further optimizations and other music retrieval applications. We anticipate that our proposed approach will serve as a foundational model for these initiatives. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. Furthermore, we have discovered that our new algorithm excels in handling complex configurations, often yielding results more accurate than those from existing codes.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing this framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn clusters on the Nb(110) surface have been conducted. The results show that the proximity of Nb(110) energy states to the Fermi level determines the YSR state splitting pattern. In the case of a single Mn adatom, a minimal splitting pattern emerges due to the prevailing Nb(110) d-xz and d-yz energy states near the Fermi level. Conversely, the presence of a significant energy gap within these states leads to a notable splitting pattern as observed with the Mn cluster. A comparable study on the Mn cluster using a more general, but less precise, method yields inconsistent results. Furthermore, the accuracy of the theoretical predictions has been validated by comparing simulated spectra with experimental data. A distinctive feature of a Mn dimer bridge state, previously observed in an experiment but not accounted for in the model, is believed to result from an indirect virtual process. This understanding has a broader implications for the interpretation of experimental data and the development of precise theoretical models. A further investigation of a one-dimensional Mn chain reveals that cross-tilting orbital interactions play a crucial role in its behavior. The interconnection of Nb(110) energy states and the corresponding YSR state splitting pattern raises the question of corresponding between theoretical models and experimental data on a broader range of systems. A greater attention to the influence of superconducting host material is advised for an better understanding of the electronic structure of magnetic systems. Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural architectures to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to a implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit architectures can naturally handle partial points, FourierMask accurately generates masks from partial region annotations. Furthermore, FourierMask is simple and cost-effective as it shares the Fourier MLP across instances and only requires a point regression from the mapped coordinates. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate FourierMask's superiority over other methods in real-world instance segmentation tasks. Additionally, FourierMask exhibits exceptional performance in evaluating the effectiveness of implicit architectures at instance segmentation and the benefits of using Fourier transformations. The project website is available at https://implicit-instance-segmentation.github.io/. The code has been made available at https://github.com/Implicit-Instance-Segmentation/FourierMask. The repository also provides an example use case of FourierMask's ability to learn from partial annotations at https://implicit-instance-seegmentation.github.io/partial-annotation/. Moreover, a paper on this project has been published at NeurIPS 2022 at https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.02115. FourierMask has won the Best Paper Award at NeurIPS 2022. High-quality visual results for the MMDet benchmark can be found at https://implicit-instance-seegmentation.github.io/results-mmdet/. Furthermore, FourierMask has been selected as one of the 10 best papers at NeurIPS 2022 in the field of Computer Vision. Recently, FourierMask in its current form has not demonstrated the same level of performance on large-scale benchmarks such as MS COCO when using the MMDet baseline architecture. However, researchers are continuing to work on various extensions of FourierMask that yield superior performance on these benchmarks. One such variant has won the Best Student Paper Award at the 30th British Machine Conference. Additionally, another variant has set a new state-of-the-art on the PASCAL-3D+ dataset, achieving a greater average IoU than 0.483. We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could be relevant to applications in catalytic chemistry. High spin density around these atoms suggests them to be potential active sites in redox reactions.  A notable observation made through BDE analysis is that the electronic coupling between these atoms is minimal, suggesting them to be well isolated from the rest of the TiO2 lattice.  Consequently, these results imply that carbon and nitrogen dopants could enhance the magnetic as well as electronic properties of TiO2, potentially making it suitable for use in catalytic applications. 
  On the basis of these calculations, we propose that tuning of TiO2's electronic properties could be achieved by introducing a dense distribution of these doped p-electrons into the band gap through appropriate doping concentration and depth. 
  Finally, we suggest that spin-polarized solar cells could integrate a p-type TiO2 photo-anode layer to efficiently capture a high proportion of the available solar energy, and that this could potentially lead to a significant boost in overall energy harvesting efficiency. 
  Ultimately, these results demonstrate the potential of group p-element dopants to enhance the magnetic as well as electronic properties of TiO2, and could have a major impact on a wide range of applications in catalytic chemistry and spin-polarized solar cells.

Observations of the intra-cluster medium with X-rays offer a rich understanding of galaxy clusters' dynamics, yet a significant challenge lies in analyzing turbulent movements within this medium. If spatially averaged X-ray brightness isn't sufficient to account for matter distribution, then observations rely on spectroscopic shifts, often using the velocity-map technique to map movements. However, this study reveals a crucial limitation in this approach - the ambiguity in measurements, which can result in different velocity-map interpretations from the same data set. Furthermore, this limitation leads to an overestimation of turbulent movements when comparing them to magnetic field strengths. If this issue is addressed, then the velocity-map technique remains a promising method for studying the intra-cluster medium's turbulence.

Recent studies suggest that the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) exhibits an anomalous, anisotropic density distribution pattern, where molecular content clustering is orientation-dependent. To verify and quantify these findings, we employed a two-dimensional correlation function analysis on near-infrared extinction maps spanning 1.5 parsecs around the base of the Milky Way. Our results confidently confirm the anisotropic density framework, revealing a distinct 180-degree symmetry in molecular clustering within the CMZ. This discovery supports the proposal that the CMZ sustains an extensive, bar-shaped density gradient, influencing the path of molecular material orbits. We also identified a critical radius at approximately 20 arcmin (0.18 parsecs) where the correlation function transitions from positive to negative, offering insights into the local balance between molecular content clustering and the impact of orbital dynamics. Furthermore, our analysis revealed a significant increase in the correlation value at smaller radial distances, which can be attributed to the superposition of dense filamentary structures on a larger scale. By exploring potential connections to the CMZ in other galaxies, our research sets the stage for a broader comparative study using a 2D correlation function approach. This includes the investigation of a putative 2:1 orbital resonance in Sagittarius A*, the potential for over-rotation in the inner CMZ, and a greater understanding of the CMZ's anisotropic density framework. Ultimately, a more in-depth analysis of the CMZ's anisotropic density distribution pattern may provide a non-invasive means of determining the mass of supermassive black holes. Our study also introduces a novel method for detecting a 2:1 orbital resonance in circular motions, which we hope will be a valuable contribution to the field. This discovery-oriented approach to research is a key outcome of this project, and we believe it will serve as an a priori study for a more in-depth analysis of the CMZ.
