This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to identify Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their afflicted eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on eye movements rather than entire facial images. This unique approach ensures individuals' anonymity and facilitates the interpretability of AI-driven conclusions. We have devised a novel metric called blink similarity, quantifying the similarity between blinking patterns, and successfully demonstrated its reliability through rigorous experiments requiring minimal labeled data. Notably, our eye-centered detection method boasts exceptional performance even in the absence of explicitly labeled paddle regions within blink annotations. Our innovative technique has immense potential to enhance the diagnosis and monitoring of Bell's Palsy via automated analysis of blinking patterns in videos. To facilitate further research, we are releasing a new, large-scale dataset called EyeBell, comprising over 14,000 high-quality video clips with accompanying eye region heatmaps and annotations for blink onset and offset times. This dataset will also be useful for developing more advanced eye activity analysis tools. Building upon our work, other researchers can leverage our insights and EyeBell dataset to create more sophisticated models integrating contextual information, such as temporal dynamics and spatial relationships among eye regions. We have already explored early iterations of such integrated approaches and observed promising results. Nonetheless, we believe that our eye-centered detection method represents a significant breakthrough in identifying Bell's Palsy through automated analysis of blinking patterns in videos. To appreciate the method's effectiveness, we have included a companion website featuring an interactive demonstration available at https://eyebell.github.io/. This method has also been selected for presentation at the CVPR 2022 workshop titled 'Recent Advances in Medical Video Analysis: Subvol 3' held in Nashville, Tennessee, USA. We are proud to say that our work has inspired a follow-up paper titled 'Eye Activity Analysis for Bell's Palsy Diagnosis: From Traditional Machine Learning to Contrastive Learning', which will be presented at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2023. To study Quantum Electrodynamics in strong-field environments, researchers have been using positron production as a key indicator. Positrons are typically generated through the interaction of extremely intense lasers with foil targets in two distinct methods: direct creation from the field and generation from accelerated electrons. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach, involving a new source of dense polarized positrons. It is proposed that accelerating electrons pass through a linearly polarized laser field as they travel, forcing the produced positrons to be polarized. In our simulation, a $10^{22} \mathrm{W}/\mathrm{cm}^2$ laser beam irradiates a thin film target at $\sim 10.2$ electron volts, and the results indicate that positrons with a high level of polarization (approximately $70\%$) can be achieved over an extensive range of parameters. Notably, our simulation demonstrates that the polarization of the positrons is largely unaffected by the irrelevance of the positron production quasi-static approximation, which holds true for high-density production in our scenario. In fact, the polarization of the positrons is shown to be resistant to variations in the polarization of the parent electrons, and it is largely maintained throughout the electron's full acceleration period. In addition, our research implies that the detection of the polarization of the positrons is feasible with a scanning magnetic field of approximately $\sim 3$ teslas. In conclusion, our study provides a new perspective on the creation of polarized positrons in laboratory settings, and it highlights the potential of positron production to serve as an effective probe of QED in strong-field environments. Furthermore, our research brings us one step closer to controlling the creation of polarized positrons, which could have a significant impact on our understanding of high-energy physics. Lastly, our study suggests that the use of film targets rather than solid targets may be advantageous, and it raises the possibility of further improving the accuracy of this technique by employing a more complex model that takes into account the intricacies of the target material. In the future, we plan to investigate the properties of the polarized positrons in more detail, with a focus on identifying potential signatures that could distinguish them from their unpolarized counterparts. For a finite group G, the polynomial width is defined as the minimum degree d such that any subgroup of G can be expressed as the union of d distinct left cosets. We have obtained the following key findings: it holds that the polynomial width of a finite group is either 1 (indicating all subgroups are right unions of single cosets) or equals the order of the group. The significant disparity between computing systems and applications at the turn of the century led to a call for action from prominent technologists, resulting in significant investments in research and development. A specific area of focus emerged in response: Grid computing, which aimed to reinvent the concept of computing as a shared resource. We examine the evolution of Grid computing, criticizing its limitations and highlighting the opportunities missed due to an overemphasis on low-level system programming. Contrary to the difficulties faced by Grid computing, our analysis finds that a similar set of applications and challenges existed during the same period, yet instead of Grid computing, the term "cluster computing" became widely used. We propose that the success of cluster computing can be attributed to its more practical approach, which focused on providing a higher-level abstraction to hide the complexities of computer systems. We explore how applying this same philosophy could have avoided the complexities associated with Grid computing and led to its early adoption. Finally, we reflect on the long-term effects of these technological developments on the field of computer science, observing how the term "cloud computing" is now being redefined to align with the same transformational approach that successfully paved the way for cluster computing. As we enter an era where the boundaries between computers and applications are once again blurring, we must consider the opportunity to apply this same transformational approach to develop a new, more versatile form of computing that can seamlessly integrate these interconnected devices. We propose the term "mobile computing 2.0" to describe this new type of environment, characterized by the coexistence of computers and applications that are no longer distinct. We also examine current projects that are shaping the future of mobile computing 2.0, discussing the technical challenges that these initiatives are addressing and the potential they hold for ushering in a new era of innovation. We anticipate that this article will spark a debate within the research community, prompting prominent technologists to invest in the development of better technologies that can efficiently manage the complexities of computer systems and provide a shared resource computing architecture that is both robust and simple to use. We anticipate that these advancements will not only give rise to a new generation of applications that can seamlessly integrate computers and programs but also create opportunities for further breakthroughs that could lead to a deeper understanding of the concept of time, the development of more effective algorithms, and the discovery of hidden patterns within large datasets. We are confident that this study will also serve as a valuable reference for those interested in learning about the evolution of shared resource computing and the opportunities that it presents. A new model for unified dark matter and energy has been developed, utilizing a complex non-linear equation of state that combines a logarithmic form for the non-interacting dark matter component and a quadratic form for the interacting dark energy component, which is influenced by a constant interaction factor. This model replaces the traditional cosmological constant model and linear vacuum energy model, and is supported by several pieces of observational data, including the cosmic microwave background radiation, type Ia supernovae, cosmic velocity data, and the matter power spectrum. A thorough analysis of the model's parameters using the Bayesian method resulted in a highly reliable set of values, which effectively reproduce the observed characteristics of a universe that is expanding at a constant rate. Furthermore, the model's ability to explain the similar densities of dark matter and energy, despite their vastly different evolution paths, has been physically justified. This justification is based on the model's assumption that the density of dark matter is directly proportional to the square of the Hubble constant, and its validity has been confirmed through a numerical analysis. A more precise calculation of the model's parameters using a Monte Carlo method based on type Ia supernovae data also resulted in a reliable set of values, which reproduce the observed characteristics of a universe that is expanding at a constant rate. Additionally, a comparison of this model to the conventional lambda-CDM model has been performed, and both models are consistent with all the observed data. However, a Monte Carlo Markov Chain analysis using type Ia supernovae data alone has previously led to an inconsistent result for the model's Hubble constant parameter. A more detailed analysis of this issue has revealed that the typical value of the interaction factor in this model, which is typically around 4.0, is also consistent with the data from the Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation experiments, and specifically with the combination of data from the BOOMERANG and DASSAULI experiments; this value indicates that the model's constant interaction factor should be declared a nuisance parameter in future analyses. Lastly, this model admits a physical interpretation that resembles the idea of creation of matter and energy during the Big Bang period, but suggests that this process should be viewed as a residual effect of the universe's initial condition rather than a process occurring throughout the universe's evolution. Ultimately, both statistical and physical justification support the validity of this model. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One understudied aspect of curiosity is its link to peer interactions.  Our study introduces a pioneering theoretical framework that combines cognitive and social factors to explain how peers can inspire curiosity through various observable behaviors and underlying states.  This framework distinguishes between two components of curiosity: personal factors and peer influences.  Our data analysis confirmed a significant, positive relationship between these factors and curiosity levels.  Additionally, our results highlighted key behaviors that contribute to curiosity in learning environments.  Building on these findings, we developed practical strategies that can be incorporated into learning technologies to identify, stimulate, and guide curiosity in real-time.  Our work is a significant step towards designing more effective learning technologies that recognize and respond to curiosity in collaborative learning settings and also paves the way for the development of computer support for other important cognitive and emotional skills.  Our work has been successfully demonstrated at conferences such as the International Conference of Learning Sciences (ICLS) and the ACM Conference on Human-Computer Interaction (CHI).  Currently, we are expanding our research to address the complexities of interest that are closely linked to curiosity and we are exploring new methods for capturing the dynamic nature of these concepts in dynamic learning environments.  Our study highlights the value of combining multiple data sources to improve the validity of our results and we believe that our approach can benefit other research areas that involve the analysis of complex cognitive and social processes in collaborative learning environments.  Our work has also inspired other researchers to explore similar questions in different cultural contexts and we are confident that our approach will shed new light on the underlying mechanisms that govern curiosity in learning environments.  Our data analysis focused on the complex relationships between curiosity, motivation, self-efficacy, anxiety, learning styles, personality, gender, and age and revealed interesting patterns that are consistent with our initial hypotheses.  Our results confirmed the significance of personal factors such as motivation, self-efficacy, and anxiety on curiosity levels and also uncovered the impact of learning styles, personality, gender, and age on curiosity in learning environments.  Our analysis highlighted the intricate connections between these factors and curiosity levels and our data showed that different students exhibit varying curiosity

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for analyzing complex data sets, extending traditional multivariate analysis to handle numerous variables with unclear dependencies. While Gaussian processes provide an effective way to model unknown relationships, the traditional approach relies on the use of squared exponential kernels, which can be challenging to apply to large data sets due to their computationally expensive implementation. The recent development of matrix Gaussian processes, such as Mat\'ern Gaussian processes, presents a more efficient alternative, based on the use of power exponential kernels that reduce the need for expensive scalar inversions. Although matrix Gaussian processes have been successful in various applications, their potential for handling complex data sets with irregular structures has yet to be explored. The aim of this work is to introduce matrix Gaussian processes as a novel approach for analyzing interdependent data, enabling the development of statistical models that can handle non-stationary relationships, missing values, and time series data, as well as to showcase its applicability using real-world datasets. We also compare the results to bounds derived from other processes and experiments, revealing that J/ψ invisible decays provide the most stringent constraints on light sterile neutrinos and certain dark matter models. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by applying it to intraday electricity price series from different European countries, leveraging a new R package called RODI. By exploring the spectral co-matrix of these data, we took a multivariate approach that surpasses the limitations of conventional methods. Unlike traditional methods, our approach handles multiple variables without imposing additional constraints. We uncovered distinct time-dependent patterns in the spectral co-matrix, revealing shared and unique components that provide valuable insights into the complex dynamics of intraday electricity prices. Notably, our approach identified a notable peak at the frequency of 4 hours, confirming the existence of an intraday effect, and a notable peak at the beginning and end of the trading day, capturing the impact of trading hours. We observed a persistent pattern of a Monday effect and an end-of-the-week effect, characterized by increased volatility. Our analysis also revealed a notable peak at the start and end of the summer time change, indicating how time changes influence electricity price volatility. We explored the spatial structure of our identified functional singular spectrum (FSS) components, revealing how they vary across European countries. Deep learning-based automated essay scoring systems are increasingly employed by educational institutions and testing agencies to evaluate numerous applicants, making critical decisions in the process. Yet, surprisingly, little research has focused on comprehending how these models develop and why they often yield inconsistent scores. This study aims to address this knowledge gap by investigating the performance of advanced essay scoring models, specifically those using neural networks. Our analysis revealed that these models exhibit both excessive sensitivity and instability, producing similar scores for significantly different essays and varying scores for essentially identical papers. These underlying issues hinder the models' ability to detect subtle stylistic tricks that can deceive them, leading to unreliable score validity. Our investigation attributes these problems to the models' reliance on superficial textual characteristics and their failure to adequately account for logical connections between an essay's components. In response, we propose adaptive neural network architectures that prioritize semantic understanding and coordinate score calculations across multiple, specialized networks. Our results show that these innovative architectures yield significant performance improvements, particularly in their ability to resist stylistic deception and ensure score coherence. The global persistence of a one-dimensional random walk's local time was analyzed over an expanding time frame. The results show that for a standard random walk, the number of distinct local time levels scales at a rate of $t^{2\ast}/3\ast^2$ as $t$ grows large, where $2\ast$ is the unique eligibility that satisfies $2\ast > 1/2$ and is obtainable through a freeness approach applied to the random walk's extended matrix model. This finding can be seen as a broader consequence of the 2019 paper by Aoun and Bercovici, where the focus here shifts towards a more general framework that includes power-regular local time levels. Additionally, the results are extended to cover random walks with non-negative increments and the simple random walk's analogs in higher-dimensional space. Fail-safe theorems are also provided, offering a more general approach to proving the main theorem. Furthermore, the results are shown to compare favorably to the persistence of one-dimensional symmetric stable random walks with index $μ>0$. Finally, the results are extended to cover the local time of one-dimensional random walks with a finite number of steps over an expanding time frame, as well as the related issue of half-space walk. Conditions for $d$-dimensional random walks to exhibit persistence in the same manner are also provided. This work is a product of collaborative efforts with David A. C. Alvarez, LeRoy D. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory treatments, resulting in potential benefits for patients with COVID-19.  By building on existing research and modeling the reaction of pyroptotic cells to treatment, our findings suggest that an individual cell can experience either apoptosis or a time-delayed pyroptotic death due to the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation.  When considering a population of cells with varying time constants for pyroptosis, our model indicates that treatment can reduce the overall delay in pyroptotic cell death, resulting in a greater population of cells undergoing pyroptosis at later time points.  This model provides a foundation for exploring more complex cellular systems and multi-scale modeling, incorporating factors such as an host-cell network and the effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection on a cellular population level. Ultimately, our research could pave the way for optimizing anti-inflammatory treatment delivery in a spatial host-cell network and across entire cellular populations.  In addition, this model can be applied to other inflammatory diseases that are induced by the formation of an NLRP3 inflammasome.  Furthermore, our study suggests that mathematical modeling in combination with confirmed experimental data on single-cell level can provide a valuable framework for exploring the effects of treatment on cellular systems.  This model offers a single-cell level understanding of how anti-inflammatory treatments modify the dynamics of pyroptosis in host cells.  In the context of COVID-19, research into the effects of treatment on an individual cell's response to SARS-CoV-2 infection is a crucial step in developing a broader population model.  As a result, this model may have implications for optimizing treatment delivery in a spatial host-cell network and across entire cellular populations.

Additionally, an algorithm is developed to remove their impact by modifying the reward signal and state variables, resulting in a new Markov Decision Process. This new process is more manageable for reinforcement learning agents to interact with. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of tests. This approach can also be combined with other reinforcement learning techniques. We also introduce a new term, "exogenous state reward," which encompasses both state and reward variables. Applying our removal algorithm results in a environment with only endogenous state rewards. This allows agents to focus on solving the resulting MDP without additional computational complexity. We explore the potential applications of this approach, acknowledging that further research is needed to fully utilize it in complex, real-world scenarios. In this research, we introduce HELMHOLTZ, a static validation tool for Tezos smart contracts built using the OCaml programming language and type theory. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in synthetic aperture imaging. However, the limited lateral resolution of this imaging method poses significant challenges. To address this issue, we propose a novel technique called Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA). VSSA involves generating multiple synthetic aperture images using virtual sources located at equal intervals across the ultrasound transducer. By analyzing the differences between these images, we demonstrate the ability to accurately estimate lateral shifts and reduce the mean absolute error by 158%. Furthermore, simulations show that VSSA's displacement estimation compares favorably to other methods, even in scenarios with significant tissue inhomogeneities. To validate the proposed technique, experiments involving a phantom and a live mouse were conducted, showing that VSSA outperforms the standard synthetic aperture method in terms of boundary detection. The results suggest that VSSA offers enhanced lateral resolution and accurate displacement estimation, making it a promising technique for elastography. To integrate VSSA with real-time imaging, a pilot study involving a phantom was also conducted, indicating that while there is room for further speed optimisation, the technique can achieve decent performance with some adjustment of parameters. The proposed method provides a viable solution to enhance the lateral resolution of ultrasound elastography. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. This combined approach holds significant potential for generating reliable and safe algorithms through a proof-based process. One practical application of this method is demonstrated through an example of developing an algorithm from first principles. Furthermore, this approach enables an interesting connection between the cut-free property and the presence of errors during program execution. If an algorithm incorporates a cut operation, it would inherently result in a non-cutoff proof, leading to an instance where the program fails to terminate or enters an invalid state. This limitation implies that all algorithms derived through this proof-based process will always possess the property of having only necessary cuts. This method offers a novel means of constructing programs with a form of "certified correctness." This approach ensures that if an algorithm fails to work as expected, it will immediately become apparent from its derivation process. This method is particularly well-suited for programs that rely heavily on side effects, as their evaluation process is inherently different from the computation of functional programs. This approach also allows for the incorporation of multiple ways to achieve a goal by integrating different algorithms that can be combined with our method. This feature enables us to leverage the fact that different algorithms can coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This approach is demonstrated through an example involving the development of an algorithm with multiple possible implementations. This approach also allows for the inclusion of user-provided functions written in another programming language, as long as the interface to these functions is clearly defined. This feature is integrated into this method through the inclusion of a demonstration that shows how to combine this approach with the Racket programming language. This combination allows for the definition of programs with a separation between the logical specification and the algorithmic implementation. This approach enables a form of modular program development, as demonstrated through an embedded video presentation. The concept of partial order is a fundamental idea in mathematics that is utilized across various disciplines, including but not limited to, geometry, topology, and algebra. A key property of partial orders is antisymmetry, which ensures that multiple elements cannot simultaneously be less than or equal to one another. In this study, we introduce a new concept known as the Boolean Ramsey property for partial orders. This property is characterized by the existence of a subset within the Boolean lattice that contains a structure isomorphic to the given partial order, and this structure appears consistently across all possible permutations of the Boolean lattice with the same number of elements. We go on to establish both upper and lower bounds for the size of the Boolean lattice required to support a Boolean Ramsey property for various types of partial orders. A key finding of this study is the determination of the optimal Boolean Ramsey number for the V-shaped poset, a result that is of a combinatorial nature with potential applications in the study of V-shaped posets in general. Additionally, this study lays out a method for a new proof of a well-known theorem regarding the density of the Boolean lattice. In the context of high-dimensional spaces, a key task in data analysis is
transforming a high-dimensional dataset into a lower-dimensional space.
A well-established approach to achieve this uses a subset of representative
points, known as a $k$-center clustering, in conjunction with the nearest
neighbor rule to map the original space. The performance of this method is
critical, as it directly influences the accuracy of subsequent analyses.
Building on previous work, which primarily focused on static scenarios, we've
developed a dynamic approach to $k$-center clustering. Our method allows
the cluster centers to shift as new data points are added or old points are
removed. Specifically, for a stream of $n$ points in $d$-dimensional space, we
select a subset of $k$ centers through an online algorithm. When the data is
spherical or linear, we prove that our algorithm results in clusters with a
neighborhood ratio of $O(k^{3/2} \log k)$, even in high-dimensional spaces.
In the case of Gaussian data, we show that our algorithm achieves a similar
performance, and and even demonstrate an lower bound of $k^{3/2}$ in some
scenarios. Our results for non-linear data, such as drawn from a mixture of
Gaussians, are also analyzed, as well as some applications of our approach
to dynamic learning and remote density estimation. Our code can be found at

Our key innovation enables the identification of a high-level strategy by categorizing regions of the environment into a hierarchy of areas of varying 'importance', allowing for more efficient exploration of the game's solution space. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in restoring standard-dose CT images from low-dose CT scans without the need for paired training data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory requirements. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently switch between producing standard-dose and low-dose CT images from the input scans. The proposed architecture achieves comparable restoration results to traditional cycleGAN methods, as evidenced by our quantitative and qualitative evaluations, while simultaneously reducing the memory requirement by 50%. Moreover, our results demonstrate that this method is on par with the state-of-the-art cycleGAN methods that employ paired data and trained on a CT range transformation task. Notably, our approach achieves this performance without the need for paired training data, making it an attractive solution for real-world clinical applications. Furthermore, our method's efficient architecture facilitates a 1.5 times increase in batch size, enabling further improvement in restoration results. The code for our AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN model has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/David-Yin/AdaIN-Switchable-CycleGAN. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure that unifies diverse annotation formats, enabling the model to focus on crucial elements for each task. To study the rotational characteristics of exotic nuclei with distorted halos, we utilized the angular momentum projection method onto the deformed mean field from the TOWIZENWANG18 potential. Our self-consistent deformed ground states and rotational states were examined for a series of neutron-rich isotopes of $^{40}$Mg, $^{44}$Mg and $^{48}$Mg. For nuclei with ground states that are highly deformed, we discovered that rotational states often exhibit shape decoupling effects, resulting from the interaction between multiple deformed configurations. Our research also indicates that halo structures are not confined to spherical or axially symmetric shapes, but can also occur in orientations that are tilted, often referred to as triangular or distorted halo states. Notably, we discovered that rotational states of distorted halo ground states tend to exhibit collective behavior similar to that of their axial counterparts, but with energy patterns that differ significantly. Moreover, our research suggests that collective features in rotational states can be probed through experimental observations of energy patterns, transition probabilities and electromagnetic moments. A theoretical framework incorporating self-consistent mean field and angular momentum projection can accurately predict the exotic properties of distorted halo nuclei. Empirical evidence from various experiments, including the non-exponential decay of the rotational state in $^{44}$Mg, the triplicate energy pattern in $^{48}$Mg and the magnetic dipole moment of $^{40}$Mg, supports our theoretical findings. Further experiments are necessary to fully explore the rotational characteristics of exotic nuclei. task destroys the previous progress on the others, hinders multi-task reinforcement
learning by preventing the learner from benefiting equally from all experiences.

In response to this challenge, we propose a sequential data collection approach with analytical formulas for balancing equality and concentration in independent and identically distributed data sets. This work analyzes the effects of the ISM on pulsar emission, specifically the pulsar B1133+16, to determine the properties of the line of sight. By examining scintillation patterns, scientists can figure out how the ISM affects the pulsar's signal and calculate the velocity of the scintillation patterns, as well as their spatial structure. A velocity of approximately 68.6 km/s was measured for the scintillation patterns, and their spatial scale was found to be around 2.5 AU. This knowledge can be used to convert the velocity of scintillation into a distance in the line of sight, allowing for an estimate of approximately 40 AU. This paper presents a novel raw waveform generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, which leverages the strengths of both autoregressive and convolutional neural networks to efficiently produce high-quality speech samples. By integrating Pitch-dependent Expanded Convolution (PDE-C) layers within the WaveNet framework, QP-Wavenet effectively captures long-range periodic patterns in speech while handling random acoustic noise. Our model's use of PDE-C layers allows it to significantly reduce memory requirements and computational costs during training, without compromising speech synthesis quality. When evaluated against a range of benchmarks, including the LJSpeech corpus, our results demonstrate near-optimal performance using the full model and also showcase the effectiveness of its simplified, non-causal variant in achieving high-quality speech synthesis with reduced memory needs. Our implementation of an autoregressive speech synthesis system, along with its memory-efficient variant, has potential applications in various speech processing tasks. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, a paper detailing our methodology has been submitted to the ICASSP 2021 conference. This model's innovative design may also be adaptable to other signal-based generative models. This research presents a novel web-based platform called MADARi, designed to synchronize morphological annotations and spelling corrections for Arabic texts. The platform offers a user-friendly interface where users can enter words and access pre-existing annotations, in addition to providing a range of tools to facilitate the annotation and correction process. MADARi accepts words written in the Latin script, converts them to Arabic script, and allows users to correct the spelling while annotating the Arabic morphological structure. The platform generates the corresponding Arabic pronunciation based on the spelling corrections and morphological annotations. To date, MADARi has accumulated a substantial collection of user-generated annotations and corrections, which are being developed into a comprehensive morphological resource. This contribution explores the design of MADARi, the resources it encompasses, and the potential it holds for collaborative annotation and the advancement of Arabic Natural Language Processing. The spell-checking feature of MADARi has been incorporated into the system used by the Royal Court of Oman for employee writing guidance. Furthermore, this platform serves as an illustration of the benefits and challenges of crowd-sourced annotation in Arabic. The development of MADARi has been supported by a grant from the Royal Court of Oman and the Oman Research Council. The platform is available at http://madari.frc.oamain.edu.om. Planets similar to Earth, orbiting nearby stars, have been found to exist in vast numbers. Many of these worlds reside within the habitable zones of their stars and are being intensively studied for their potential to support life. To effectively identify exoplanets living under conditions similar to those of Earth, researchers are using ground-based and space-based spectral analysis of their light-filtered signals. This technique is based on analyzing the absorption patterns of various gases in the atmospheres of these planets as they pass in front of their stars during orbital alignment. This paper explains the photochemical changes occurring in the atmospheres of these planets and reviews their composition as derived from spectral analysis, also outlining the current limitations and future prospects of this field of study. High levels of stellar energy break down the molecules in these atmospheres, leading to a mix of chemical elements that vary based on the atmosphere's temperature, with temperate planets experiencing a different breakdown pattern than those experiencing extreme heat. While primary gases like H2O, CH4, H2S, and CO2 are present in significant amounts, other species such as NH3, HCN, HCOOH, and CO also contribute to their composition. The complex interplay between photochemistry and host star properties remains only partially understood and new missions like PLATO, TESS, and Hubble's WFE will likely provide a more detailed understanding of these worlds, along with their potential for life. This field of study will continue to evolve over the next decade, with several new missions and studies offering further insights into exoplanet atmospheres. Multi-directional propagation through interconnected entities, inherent to processes like information diffusion and infection spread, can be analyzed using graph neural networks. Recent breakthroughs in end-to-end learning and real-world applications have propelled graph neural networks to the forefront, but most existing approaches rely on simplified linear forward propagation models, which fall short in capturing the complexities of real-world systems. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel neural network architecture called the Lorentzian graph neural network, which leverages the Bradley-Taylor similarity measure to model non-linear propagation. By extending the framework to handle inter-arrival times and degree changes, our model can learn to anticipate periods of rapid entity activation and synchronization. We demonstrate the efficacy of this model on synthetic and real-world datasets, showcasing its superiority over conventional graph neural networks. Our research also delves into analyzing the neural code behind these results. We introduce a new neural decoding method to extract the model's understanding of entity relationships and the propagation process. This approach enables us to explore the interpretation of neural representations in graph neural networks. Our implementation is available open-source at https://github.com/author/lgnn. We outline several potential applications for the model, including recommendation systems and epidemic forecasting. However, a detailed evaluation of these use cases is left for future research. Instead, we present a new problem statement related to predictive modeling. We define the terms entity activation pattern and delay pattern and discuss their relevance to our model's performance. We also introduce a metric called delay distribution entropy and provide a preliminary analysis of its effectiveness in assessing the complexity of a graph neural network's training process. We conclude by outlining several directions for future research and the broader implications of our work. We touch on the possibility of extending the Lorentzian graph neural network architecture to other application domains and the importance of further investigating the entity activation pattern and delay pattern. We emphasize the need for a more in-depth evaluation of the model's performance on a wider range of datasets and the potential risks associated with overfitting. We also discuss a related concept called the inter-arrival time distribution and the benefits of incorporating degree changes into the model. We outline several open-source repositories related to our research and highlight the limited attention given to modeling complex propagation processes in graph neural networks. We conclude by reaffirming the significance of the entity activation pattern and delay pattern in graph neural network research and the necessity for a more qualitative analysis of neural code. The Acoustic Inverse Problem, in conjunction with structural interference, has been successfully resolved using mathematical modeling. However, the presence of interfering structural information poses a major hurdle in acoustic imaging. To complicate matters, a unknown acoustic medium further obscures the problem, making it essential to develop innovative methods to tackle this challenge. In this paper, a new strategy is presented, in which the structural information is utilized in an opposite direction to that which would normally be expected. Instead of using it as a constraint, it is used to reconstruct the acoustic medium using the interfering acoustic pressure field and the knowledge of a non-zero boundary condition on the interface between the two mediums. The new approach is tested with both numerical data and a realistic scenario involving water and a solid plate with a complex shape. The results demonstrate its effectiveness compared to conventional methods and the potential it holds for addressing more complex problems. The paper concludes with possible extensions to further complications such as velocity variations in the solid medium and limited data availability. The new approach presented could also be applied to other types of inverse problems involving structural acoustic interactions. The method developed, utilizes the transformation operator and the resolvent operator, and involves the solution of a boundary integral equation that results from the weak formulation of the acoustic problem. The method has a computational cost that scales linearly with respect to the frequency parameter and a sublinear cost with respect to the resolution of the grid in the normal direction to the interface. The method is highly efficient, especially when compared to finite element methods, and holds promise for further research in this exciting and challenging area of study. The name proposed for this method is the Inverse Challenge for Structural Acoustic Interaction (ICSAI). The acronym ICSAI captures the essence of this method as it represents the difficult challenge that this method poses to conventional techniques of solving the acoustic inverse problem, especially when structural interference is present. The word 'Challenge' embodies this hard to overcome obstacle, while the word 'Acoustic' points to the acoustic component of this problem, the word 'Inverse' indicates the type of this particular problem, the word 'Structural' refers to the interfering solid medium, and the word 'Acoustic' once more highlights the imaging of this medium. The name ICSAI also provides a clear and concise summary of this method, and it is believed that this name will be well received by the scientific community. In 3D gravity, adopting a harmonic gauge condition yields multiple gauge choices, leading to a potentially infinite number of gauge variations. This issue arises because the harmonic gauge condition overlaps with the de Donder gauge's divergence-free constraint for a massless scalar field. As a result, either all harmonic gauges or none are compatible with general relativity's physical content. As an alternative to the harmonic gauge, we suggest a new set of gauge conditions that directly eliminate the overlap with the de Donder gauge, thereby resolving the problem of multiple gauge choices. Furthermore, this new gauge set possesses a simpler symmetry transformation, which is in stark contrast to the complicated relationship between the physical states in different harmonic gauges. As an additional observation, we explore the properties of linearized Hefty gravity in the harmonic gauge, revealing that the algebraic gauge dependence arises solely from the harmonic gauge's scalar component, which is absent in linearized gravity. Moreover, both the new gauge set and Hefty gravity's linearized theory yield the same physical content as the de Donder gauge. As an interesting side note, we find that the new gauge set for linearized gravity shares a fascinating connection with the harmonic gauge choice for a massless scalar field. Similarly, we also find an intriguing relationship between Hefty gravity's linearized theory in the harmonic gauge and the massive scalar field's physical states in the de Donder gauge. However, a careful examination indicates that these coincidences are purely accidental. Ultimately, our analysis emphasizes the importance of distinguishing between the vector and scalar components of the harmonic gauge condition to avoid the problem of multiple gauge choices. Additionally, we highlight that the issue of infinite gauge choices arises specifically in 3D gravity and is not a problem in higher dimensional theories. As such, our proposed new gauge set should be relevant not just to Hefty gravity but also to any higher dimensional theory that exhibits similar characteristics. In the process, we derive a novel formula for the physical state's inner product in the new gauge set, which is formulated in terms of the harmonic gauge's components. Consequently, we are able to establish a direct link between the new gauge set and the de Donder gauge, which reveals a fascinating gauge-dependent aspect of the massless scalar field's equi-energy surface. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. We introduce a new boundary-integration technique called the Swift method, enabling fast and accurate computations of Poiseuille and Stokes flows within complex planar domains by utilizing a simplified interface calculation that minimizes complex details, thereby expediting numerical simulations. By leveraging an expanded set of reference lengths, we transform the analysis into a non-dimensional form, making the algorithm remarkably robust and adaptable to various geometric configurations. Compared to established finite-element and boundary-element methods, Swift yields significant performance improvements, achieving speed-ups of over a hundred in some cases. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we apply Swift to investigate blood flow through a representative cerebral microvessel with a bifurcation point and compare its results with those obtained using MRI angiography. The Swift algorithm is openly accessible through an easily customizable Python framework on the GitHub platform. High-resolution computational data and sophisticated MRI-like visualization images are also generated using the Swift framework and are freely available on the OpenScience Framework. Ultimately, this study aims to contribute to the development of suitable blood flow simulations that can be used in realistic MRI simulations. By publicly releasing the Swift algorithm and computational data, we hope to facilitate its further improvement and provide a starting point for investigations into a broader range of flow phenomena. In particular, we encourage researchers to explore its application to flow simulations through branching vessels, turbulent flow, and the simulation of MRI sequences. The publicly available GitHub repository containing the Swift algorithm is located at the following URL: https://github.com/BIOTechLab/Swift. A companion website providing additional information and a downloadable executable version of the Swift algorithm can be found at the following URL: http://biotech.vanderbilt.edu/s-swift. High-resolution computational data and MRI-like images are available through the following DOIs: http://dx.doi.org/10.20319/datasets/2021070151 and http://dx.doi.org/10.20319/datasets/2021070152. The Swift algorithm has been successfully ported to the NGSolve platform, a high-performance numerical simulation solver developed by the FIMFAM Research Group. The combined strengths of both Swift and NGSolve have enabled the simulation of complex flow simulations on multiple CPUs and GPU devices. Additionally, Swift has been integrated with the VTK library, allowing for the direct conversion of mesh data into commonly used visualization formats. Furthermore, we have explored the application of Swift to the solution of the Helmholtz equation and have achieved comparable performance to that of established finite-element methods.
